Having first prostrated before my Guru, then to the Lord of the Gaṇas, and to the Illustrious Supreme Deity, I compose this one beautiful treatise for the delight of the great Kaulika worshippers. (1.1)

In those scriptures wherein the illustrious path of the Kula was taught in detail by Sadāśiva, they are for the most part no longer easily available in the Kali age, and their supreme knowledge is exceedingly difficult to attain. (1–2)

Where there is abundant grace from the Guru and great favor from the venerable Deity, only that man possesses knowledge of the Kula scriptures; for him alone exists devotion here, which is indeed free from the afflictions of the wicked.

Those who possess firm devotion to this scripture here and correctly understand its entire secret, having pure intellect due to the merit of previous births—for them, the worlds of those who revile it do not exist. (1.4)
Some, fearing for their own cattle, disparage this family scripture;
yet others, ignorant and devoted to censure, who are wicked by nature, shall dwell in hell. (1–5)
May firm devotion toward this scripture arise in the virtuous, whereby their respective auspiciousness may be fully realized.
Let that which exists [in one] not be obstructed by another scripture; indeed, one ought not to be a reviler. (1–6)

The two paths known as the right and the left are established by numerous statements and by all the scriptures of the Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas; they are both valid according to the distinctions of their respective conventions and so forth. (1.7)

May the Kaulas become happy upon beholding this treatise named *Kūlapradīpa*, which is endowed with the causes for attaining Brahman, is worthy of being heard, and constitutes the essence of all the Agamas. 1-8.
In that regard, first is the praise of the family dharma (*kuladharma*). From the *Śrīkulārṇava*:
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Kula, O ocean of compassion for all beings, I desire to hear [more].
O God, you have merely indicated the Kula-dharma; you have not yet revealed it.
O Supreme Lord, if you have any affection for me, tell me the majesty of that Dharma, which is the highest of all Dharmas. 1-10.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare that which you ask of me;
by the mere hearing of it, one shall become dear to the Yoginīs.
I have not previously spoken of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Guha, and the others;
out of affection for you, I shall now speak—listen with a one-pointed mind.
Transmitted through a succession of lineage, established from mouth to mouth, it is ultimately unspeakable; nevertheless, I shall tell it to you. 1-13.
You too must indeed keep it secret; it must not be given to just anyone.
It should be given to a disciple who is devoted to the teacher; otherwise, there will be a fall. 1-14.
The Vedas are superior to all [other scriptures], and the Vaiṣṇava [scripture] is indeed superior to the Vedas; the Śaiva is superior to the Vaiṣṇava, and the Dakṣiṇa is superior to the Śaiva.
The left (Vāma) is superior to the Right (Dakṣiṇa); the Siddhānta is the most excellent above the Left;
the Kaula is superior to the Siddhānta; and there is nothing higher than the Kaula.
O Goddess, it is secret, more secret than the secret, the supreme essence of essences; O Goddess, it is the lineage that has passed from ear to ear, the manifest Supreme Śiva himself. (1–17)
O Goddess, having churned the great ocean of the Vedas and Agamas with the staff of knowledge, I, who am a knower of the essence, have extracted the Kula-dharma.
On one side are all the religious duties such as sacrifices, sacred fords, and vows;
on the other side is the family dharma (kuladharma), and therein, O Beloved, the Kaula is superior.
Just as rivers carrying their trivial currents enter the ocean, even so all commitments (samayas) indeed enter into the family alone. 1-20.
Just as all the footprints of living beings are contained within the footprint of an elephant, so too all philosophical systems and all spiritual commitments are equal within this [Samaya]. (1.21)
Just as all other vehicles are not equal to that of the gods,
so too all other observances are not equal to the Kula-dharma.
Just as there is a vast difference between Mount Meru and a mere pebble, or between the sun and a firefly,
so too is the great difference between this Samaya and the Kula.
O beloved, if there exists a woman equal to you, or if there exists a man equal to me, then one may speak of equality in lineage and in dharma. (1.24)
For out of delusion, that evil-minded one might speak of family dharma as if it were the true dharma; he who is himself born abandons the Unborn, even while claiming to be his support. (1.25)
O beloved, he who out of ignorance speaks of a duty superior to that of his own family incurs a sin greater than the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
Having boarded the vessel of the family dharma, that best of men traveled to the island of heaven and attained the jewel of liberation.
In all philosophical systems, men attain liberation through long-term practice; however, in the Kaula system, they attain it immediately—of this there is no doubt.
"O beloved of my life, why do you not listen even though much has been said?
There is no one equal to you among the Kaulas; I swear it by you, O Mistress of the Kula! (1-29)
If one were a yogi but not an enjoyer, or an enjoyer but not a knower of yoga, then the Kaula—which consists of both enjoyment and yoga—would not exist; therefore, O Dear One, it is superior to all.
In the family dharma, O Mistress of the Kula, enjoyment directly becomes yoga, sin becomes merit, and even worldly existence becomes liberation. (1.31)
O Goddess, even the gods such as Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as sages and rākṣasas, are devoted to their respective family duties; what then can be said of human beings?
Having abandoned all phenomena and the various doctrines of the teachers, one should indeed know only the *kula* if one desires one's own accomplishment. (1.33)

Due to the practice performed in previous births, [the knowledge] revealed by the lineage-knowledge arises—like the memory of one who has just awakened from sleep—even without instruction or the like. (1.34)
Whatever wisdom has been acquired by men over thousands of previous births, that very same wisdom the creature regains; the mere form of the body and its location are useless. (1.35)
Through these [devotions] to Śiva, Viṣṇu, Durgā, Arka (the Sun), Gaṇapati, and the Moon-born (Śiva), the knowledge of Kaula shines forth for one whose mind is purified. (1.36)
O Goddess of the gods, all dharmas are traditionally known as returning again;
however, those who abide in the Kula-dharma are all non-returning.

O Goddess, for those men whose past sins have been exhausted through penance, charity, sacrifice, pilgrimage to sacred fords, recitation of mantras, and religious observances, the knowledge of the lineage becomes manifest.
For one whose mind is pure, who is tranquil, who abides in the Dharma, who serves the guru, and who is devoted—even if he is a secret practitioner—the Kaula knowledge shines forth. (1.39)
To one who possesses true existence, who is rich in joy, who is firm in vows regarding right conduct,
who observes the commands of the Guru, who is blessed, and who has manifested the Kaula knowledge— || 1.40 ||
Knowledge of the lineage never remains in one who is unworthy;
therefore, after examination, the knowledge of the lineage spoken by me should be declared. (1.41)
One should not speak the Śiva-dharma, the teaching of Śiva, to an unworthy person;
by violating the command, one would incur shame and receive the curse of the deity. || 1.42 ||

If one speaks of the family dharma (*kuladharma*) without understanding the conduct of the pledge (*samayācāra*), both the guru and the disciple shall become mere beasts (*paśu*) in the eyes of the yoginīs. (1.43)
Having awakened the disciple, the Guru should reveal the knowledge of the Kula;
he then directly attains that union of Yoginīs and Vīras, which is the manifestation of the Goddess Tābūbhau.
He who crosses the ocean of saṃsāra without effort—having understood this family dharma—is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (1.45)
One who travels the great path of the family dharma shall go to the city of liberation; of this there is no doubt, and it will happen before long. Therefore, one should practice the Kaula way. 1-46.
He who, disregarding the Kula scriptures, practices the scriptures of the bound (paśu), is a fool who wanders for alms while his own home is full of cooked rice. (1.47)
He who abandons the noble dharma and becomes devoted to the dharma of beasts is like one who, casting away a jewel held in his hand, longs for a fragment of glass. (1.48)
He who abandons the mantras of his own lineage and practices the mantras of the beasts is like one who, having cast aside a heap of grain, desires to grasp a mound of dust. (1.49)
He who disregards his own family and looks instead toward the lineage of others is like one afflicted by thirst who abandons a pond and runs toward a mirage.
O Mistress of the Kula, other traditions besides the glorious Kaula are like the water of a magician’s net on a path; they bring pleasure for only a moment. (1.51)
The foolish person who desires liberation while remaining ignorant of his own family dharma is like one who seeks to cross the shoreless ocean from this side to the other using only his two hands.

Or whoever, desiring both worldly enjoyment and liberation according to other philosophical systems, [seeks them] as if with wealth obtained in a dream, like one who has lost his wealth in a dream. (1.53)
O Pārvatī, just as the delusion of silver may arise in mother-of-pearl, so too, enjoyment and liberation are praised as resulting from other systems of convention. (1.54)
O Mistress of the Kula, even one who has lost all ritual actions and is devoid of caste and stage of life,
yet remains devoted to the Kula, is a worthy recipient of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Even one devoid of knowledge of the Kula attains prosperity through devotion to the Kula; a woman reaches that same state, so what need be said of one who is devoted to it as his supreme goal? 1.56
O beloved, when neglected, family dharma destroys; when protected, it protects;
when honored, it quickly honors. Therefore, one should not abandon it.
"Let all my kinsmen revile me; let my wife, sons, and others abandon me; let people look upon me with contempt, or let kings punish me. (1.58)
One should serve, serve again, and continue to serve you alone, O supreme deity; I shall never speak against your Dharma through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
O Goddess, even one who has fallen into such adversity, if his intellect remains well-settled, he is honored in the world beyond and shall become auspicious. (1.60)
O Śivā, even one who is constantly afflicted by disease, poverty, suffering, and the like,
shall attain the eternal state if they worship you with devotion.
Let people praise or revile; let Fortune stay or depart;
whether death occurs today or at the end of the age, one should never abandon one's family.
He who, though born into a family tradition, does not honor you, is censured from the very moment of his birth as a burden upon the earth and an enemy to himself. (1.63)
Like shriveled grains among the crops, or like chaff among living beings, or like bubbles upon the waters—those who turn their backs on the Kaula path are such. (1.64)
For even trees live, and deer and birds live;
yet he whose mind is set upon living truly lives, being established in the dharma of his lineage.
For one who has fallen away from the family dharma, days come and go;
though he breathes, he does not truly live, like a blacksmith’s bellows filled with iron slag. (1.66)
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping, the life of one who knows the Command of Kula is like that of a beast, O Mistress of Kula. (1.67)
Even a learned man is a fool, and even a righteous man is unrighteous, and even one established in vows is without vows—if he is a person who turns his back on the Kaula path. (1.68)
O Goddess, only those born who are devoted to their family dharma and live as virtuous beings are truly living creatures in this world; the rest are merely asses in bellies.
Those devoted to the dharma of their lineage are called *suṣumā* by the virtuous;
the other, however, is the *para-pṛṣṭya*, covered with the skin of a fish and a heap of grain.
O Dear One, one who knows the arts of the four Vedas is inferior to a Śvapaca;
however, a Śvapaca who knows his own lineage excels even a Brāhmaṇa and the others.
Purified by the compassion of the Guru and cleansed of all impurities through initiation,
O Goddess, he who delights in the worship of the Kula is the true body of the body, and none other.
O unvenerated one, when a Kaulika does not perceive the knowledge of the Kula and does not worship the Śākta, his life is like that of a crow. 1.73.
They are worthy of worship, they are performers of meritorious deeds, they are the virtuous, and they are yogis—
those by whose good fortune, O Goddess, the knowledge of the Kula is revealed.
Blessed are they, those great-souled ones, the best of men, who have accomplished their purpose, in whose minds arises the knowledge of the lineage as proclaimed by me. (1.75)
Going to all sacred precincts, bathing in all holy fords, performing all sacrifices, and entering into the duties of one’s own lineage; || 1.76 ||
Those men who enter the family dharma and are not unrighteous never again enter a mother’s womb.
Even by mere incidental contact, O Goddess, whatever family one may lead to the Kulakula,
that family becomes the Kula through your grace.
O Mistress of the Kula, for one who knows the Kula, there is no need for other dharmas;
likewise, for one who does not know the Kula, there is also no need for other dharmas. (1.79)
To the high-souled Kaulikas who are devoted to the Kula and Akula, I shall impart the supreme knowledge at the time of my final departure; of this there is no doubt.
Alas, people, longing for the time when the Kalpa has long since passed, do not recognize that the Kaula tradition bestows all fruits with ease! 1-81.
For one who knows the lineage is indeed omniscient, even if he has not studied the Vedas or the Shastras;
whereas one who knows the Vedas, Shastras, and Agamas, yet does not know the lineage, is truly ignorant. (1.82)
Only your devotees, and no others, know the greatness of your lineage;
only those with the brilliance of the moon’s luster understand the beauty of the letter *ca*, and no others.
O Dear One, having heard the discourse on the family (*kula*), they find satisfaction in the knowledge of the family alone;
do small ponds ever increase like the ocean by means of moonlight? (1.84)
Those of noble lineage, though burdened by suffering, do not look to any other dharma, just as bees that enjoy the fragrance of the mandāra flower do not seek out another flower. (1.85)
For all the wise honor family traditions, as do others; look how Śiva bears the moon upon his head, and how the lion holds the moon in its mouth! (1.86)
Only those with supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) know the lineage of descent; those without such knowledge do not.
Does a bird know how to drink water mixed with milk? "I shall swallow it"—does it think so? (1.87)
The world consists of Śiva and Śakti and is established in the Kaula;
therefore, how could the Kaula not be superior to all and the common support of everything? (1.88)
These six are my limbs: the feet, the belly, the hands, and the head;
whoever should cause injury to them is indeed a cutter of my limbs. (1.89)
For these very same six limbs belong to the Kula as well;
therefore, O Dear One, the Kaula is identical with Me, and I am identical with the Kaula.
O beloved, in this lineage of Ambā, there is a single deity who grants the fruit of all philosophical systems without exception, and who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Even though it contradicts worldly norms, the Kula attains the status of valid authority in the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*, because it yields perceptible results. (1.92)
And direct perception, O beloved, is the most excellent among all means of valid cognition; by its forceful apprehension, all sophists are defeated. (1.93)
Who can authorize what is beyond the senses, or what indeed will come to pass?
Only that which yields immediate fruit is the supreme vision.
"Knowing this family dharma, all human beings are liberated.
Thinking thus, O Maheśānī, I have [proclaimed] what is censured in the world. (1-95)
For one whose affliction by evil karma in a previous birth is excessive, the guru’s compassion does not reach them, and the Kaula knowledge does not arise. (1.96)
For those who are devoid of compassion, who oppose the knowledge of the Kula, who are like beasts, and who lack true understanding, the Kula-dharma is held in contempt. (1.97)
Just as those who are blind do not see the sun, the illuminator of all,
so too those deluded by your *māyā* do not recognize your lineage.
Human beings constantly worship the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, and other philosophical systems with extreme devotion, as if they were the fruits of their labor.
Alas! Fools deride this vision of Yours, which is declared in the Vedas and Shastras as the sole means for both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and which is so dear to You. 1-100.
O Goddess, millions of scriptures have been examined by me, yet there are those who do not know the Kula-dharma; they possess a vain pride in their own knowledge. (1.101)
Indeed, all the scriptures concerning animal sacrifice were spoken by me alone; having assumed another form, I taught them for the delusion of the evil-minded. (1.102)
Due to the power of great sins, a desire for those [objects] arises in men;
indeed, for them there is no attainment of a good state even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Even when being urged on, a person of sinful nature does not engage in noble conduct; even when being restrained, a person of virtuous nature adheres only to the family tradition.
By virtue of their family duty, the gods have undertaken the role of messengers;
yet sages, lords of yoga, and others have attained supreme perfection.

Those on this earth who are devoted to animal sacrifices and the like, who are easily found, and who are hypocrites—even though they may profess to follow the Kaula path—they are not great; for those who truly serve the Kaula way are indeed rare.
There are many men who speak falsely regarding the meaning of reality; O Mistress of the Kula, one who is truly proficient in the principles of the Kula is rare to find.
The sight of one who observes the conduct of the family is rare throughout all the worlds;
it is obtained only as the ripening of merits, O beloved, and not otherwise.
O Pārvatī, all the Kula scriptures have been spoken by me alone;
they are authoritative, of this there is no doubt, and they must not be refuted by means of logical arguments.
Thus concludes the praise of the family dharma (*kuladharma*).
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Kulapradīpa* composed by the venerable Śivānandācārya. 1.
The Second Chapter: Now, the Praise of the Kaulikas.
There is no other merit equal to the Kula-worship in the three worlds.
Therefore, he who worships with devotion is the recipient of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (2-1)
Even one who has not studied and is ignorant of the scriptures, if he is devoted to his guru, firm in his vows, and intent on the worship of his lineage, shall become most dear to me. (2.2)
O Goddess, those whose hair stands on end and whose voices become faltering with joy when their lineage is being proclaimed— such are said to be the lords of the Kaulikas.
"The family dharma (kuladharma) proclaimed by Śiva is superior to all dharmas in the world"—those whose intellects are certain of this are called the best of the Kaulikas. (2.4)
O Dear One, he who knows the reality of the Kula, is proficient in the Kula-dharma, and is devoted to the worship of the Kula, should be a Kaulika; [others] are hypocrites. (2.5)
He who is pleased upon seeing those devoted to the family, those who follow family conduct, those who possess family knowledge, and those who observe family vows— he, the Kaulika, is dear to me.
Whether remembered, praised, seen, saluted, or even addressed, he purifies— even if he be a Cāṇḍāla— whomever he meets by chance, provided he is devoted to his family dharma.
Whether he be omniscient or a fool, whether he be the highest or even the lowest— O Goddess, wherever there is one who possesses the knowledge of the Kula, there I am also, together with you.
"I do not dwell on Kailāsa, nor on Meru, nor in a temple;
O beautiful woman, I reside wherever those who possess the knowledge of the lineage abide. (2.9)
One who knows the reality of the three principles, the meaning of the root-mantra of the venerable feet,
and is devoted to the deity and the guru, becomes a Kaulika through initiation by the river.
O Mistress of the Kula, wherever a Kulayogin who follows the true path may wander,
one should go even a great distance if there is a person devoted to Maheśvara.
And he should be sought with effort; whether he is present there or situated at a great distance, this family preceptor (kuladeśika) must be seen. (2-12)
O beloved, even if one is nearby, a mere beast should not be looked upon;
rather, that place where there is a knower of the Kula and people who partake in merit [should be seen]. (2-13)
By seeing and worshipping him, one shall uplift twenty-one generations of one's family;
having beheld the knower of the lineage (kulajñānin) residing in his own household, [one achieves this].
All the ancestors dance, thinking, "We shall go to the supreme goal";
the ancestors rejoice completely, like those who have seen a well-timed rain.
In such families, whether it be a son or a grandson, there shall be one who is a Kaulika;
indeed, he is a fortunate man in this world, his impurities having been destroyed. (2-16)
O Dear One, when the Kula-teachers approach with joy, the Kaulikas likewise proceed toward their own assembly once the Lord of the Kaulas has arrived. (2.17)
O Goddess, the Yoginīs arrive joyfully together with the Yogins;
having entered the Lord of Kulayogins, the Pitṛs and the deities enjoy [the feast]. (2-18)

Therefore, one should worship others with devotion within the knowledge of the Kula; for those who, having worshipped you, O Goddess, do not worship [others] out of devotion to you—[they are at fault]. (2.19)
Those who are wicked are not worthy recipients of what has been given by you;
whatever is done for those who are the ruin of their families is as if it were done for the gods.
All the gods are dear to the Kula; therefore, one should worship the Kaulika.
Even when well-worshipped with such devotion elsewhere, I am not so pleased. (2.21)
O Pārvatī, hear how I am properly pleased when honored by the Kaulikas;
O beloved, hear what fruit one obtains from the worship of the lords of the Kaulikas. (2.22)

O Ambikā, one shall not obtain that fruit through pilgrimages, austerities, charity, self-restraint, vows, nor through what is given, sacrificed, offered in fire, muttered in prayer, worshipped, or endured.
O Goddess, for one who would honor a Kaulika [only] out of worldly vanity, that house of his is a cremation ground, like ashes scattered about. (2.24)
Whatever one may give according to one's ability to a Kulayogin with affection on special lunar days, the fruit of that cannot even be calculated. (2.25)
O Goddess, on an auspicious day, one who knows the lineage of the Ādiga family should personally worship the deity with devotion using perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and other offerings. (2.26)
One should satisfy them with true devotion by means of the five mudrās beginning with wine;
when they are satisfied, I am satisfied, and all the deities shall be satisfied. (2-27)
O Goddess of the Gods, the merit of one who gives his sister, daughter, or wife to a yogin of noble family who is intoxicated with honey cannot be calculated. (2-28)
Unplanted yet sown, growing without effort, this honey offered from the mouths of heroes is the provisions for the journey to the next world. (2.29)
For family wealth entrusted to the lord of the family protects even one who is joined with evil conduct and excluded from all the world. (2.30)
O beloved, even that land where a hero devoted to the worship of his family lineage resides becomes purified; how much more so for one who stands before him! (2-31)
When even a single devotee of the Lord of the Kaulas attains merit, it becomes ten millionfold;
how much more so when many are liberated—that merit can indeed not be calculated.
Therefore, with every effort, in all circumstances and at all times, one should delight in the family dharma and worship those who possess knowledge of the family. || 2-33 ||
He who is not affected by blame or praise, cold or heat, pleasure or pain, and so forth, even among his kinsmen— he is a lord of yogis, free from both joy and dejection.

Free from conceptualization and mental construction, with all limiting adjuncts dissolved due to the cessation of latent impressions, the yogi—devoid of the illusion of his own nature—is a knower of the supreme reality. (2.35)
O Mistress of the Kula, just as those who are lame, blind, mute, impotent, or dull-witted dwell [in the world], so too does the yogi who knows reality. (2.36)
He who abides, filled with supreme bliss arising from the five mudrās, beholding the Self within the self—he indeed is the lord of yogins. (2.37)
He who always delights in meat and liquor, who always contemplates the feet [of the Guru], and who is always free from doubt—he is called a Kulayogin. (2.38)
Drinking wine, eating meat, and devoted to acting according to my own will,
I dwell in happiness, contemplating the identity between the two as being within myself.
He whose mouth is devoid of all fragrance of food is one who must perform penance and is to be shunned by all; he is nothing but a beast, without a doubt. (2.40)
As long as there is the scent of animal flesh, even Paśupati himself is but an animal;
without the scent of meat, he is truly the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati). (2.41)
In the world, the base is the sublime, and the sublime is the base;
this has been declared by the great-souled Bhairava in the Kula path. (2.42)
O Mistress of the Kula, for those of the Kaula lineage, improper conduct is always proper conduct, what is not to be done is the highest duty, and even untruth becomes truth. (2.43)

O Mistress of the Kula, for the followers of the Kaula path, even that which is undrinkable may become drinkable, and likewise that which is unfit to be eaten becomes edible; even that which is unapproachable becomes approachable. (2.44)
O Mistress of the Kula, for the Kaulikas there is neither injunction nor prohibition, neither merit nor sin, neither heaven nor indeed hell. (2.45)
Even enemies become friends, and kings serve them directly;
all people act as kinsmen for those born into the Kālikā lineage, O Mistress of the Family (Kuleśvarī). (2.46)

O Mistress of the Kula, for those of the Kaula lineage, even those with foul faces become fair-faced, all who were arrogant bow down, and even those who cause obstacles act as spiritual helpers. (2.47)

In the lineage of the Kaulikas, O Mistress of the Family, even base qualities become excellent qualities, the family-less becomes possessed of family, and even unrighteous acts become righteous. (2.48)
O Goddess, for those of the Kaula lineage, O Mistress of the Family, death acts as a physician, heaven itself acts as a home, and non-attachment acts as merit. (2.49)
Those who lack higher knowledge perceive it as higher knowledge, and those who are poor perceive it as wealth;
even when ruined, the weavers prosper under the leader of the clan. (2.50)
O Dear One, what is the use of much speaking here? The lord of the kula-yogins is always perfected through his resolve; no further deliberation is required in this matter. (2.51)
In whatever guise and unobserved by anyone, the Kulayogin proceeds, dwelling in whatever hermitage he may find. (2.52)
Yogins, who benefit human beings through various guises, wander upon this earth with their true nature unrecognized. (2.53)
Just as in the world the movement of the sun and moon and the course of the stars in the sky is imperceptible, so too is the conduct of yogins. (2.54)
Just as the path of birds in the sky and of aquatic creatures in the water cannot be seen, so too is the conduct of the great-souled ones.
Those skilled in the family yoga speak as if they were non-existent; they should conduct themselves in such a way that people do not even think of them, so as to avoid attachment. (2.56)
O Mistress of the Kula, the wise Kulayogin who moves about like one liberated, skilled in playing with children, should speak like a madman. (2.57)
Just as this world laughs, loathes, and reviles [the yogi], and avoids him from afar upon seeing him, so does the yogi conduct himself. (2.58)
In some places refined, in some places roasted, and in some places like a bhūta or piśāca, the yogi, assuming various guises, should wander upon the great earth. (2.59)
The yogi, for the benefit of the world, enjoys pleasures without longing; bestowing grace upon all people, he sports upon the surface of the earth. (2.60)
Just as the sun consumes everything and just as the fire devours all things, so too the yogi, having enjoyed all pleasures, remains unstained by sin. (2.61)
Just as water from a village becomes pure when it joins a river, so too food and other items from the house of a mleccha become pure when placed into the hand of a yogi. (2.62)
O Goddess of the gods, by the offering of a drop (*bindu*) to a Kaulika, one obtains the fruit of giving away ten million maidens and a hundred loads of gold. (2.63)
If one gives the second [offering] joined with the first to a family-yogin, all the Mothers, Yoginīs, Bhairavas, and others are satisfied. (2.64)
Whatever fruit one might obtain by giving away the earth filled with gold, ten thousand times that merit is obtained by giving [this] during the Kali age. (2.65)
A Brahmin obtains the merit of the horse sacrifice and other rites performed for the great sages through the gift of food; he gains that same fruit by giving with the *mudrā* in the Kaula tradition.
O Goddess, the merit that a man obtains by the gift of ten million cows,
that same merit belongs to the giver of the fifth [initiation] in the Kaulika tradition.
O Goddess, a Kaulika obtains through the union with Śakti that same merit which is gained by bathing at sacred fords thirty-five million times. (2.68)
Having beheld [the deity] according to the *Māheśvara* section of the *Brahmayāmala*, one should worship him according to the prescribed rule;
and having offered the five principles (*pañcatattva*) with the previously mentioned ritual, according to one's means. (2.69)
Then indeed, O Goddess, one shall obtain all desires;
otherwise, there will be no success at all, and Caṇḍikā becomes enraged. (2.70)
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving away the entire earth to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
that same fruit is obtained in the worship of the Kaulika.
The fruit that one obtains by witnessing thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices is attained through the worship of the Kaulika.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving gold equal in weight to Mount Meru to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, that same fruit is obtained through the worship of the Kaulika.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by constructing ponds, wells, tanks, and the like,
that fruit is multiplied a hundred-thousandfold by worshipping the Kaulikas.
He who, though devoted to the Kula scriptures, reviles the Kaulika, goes to a terrible hell; this is the truth, there is no doubt. (2.75)
Thus ends the praise of the Kaulikas. Now follows the praise of the Kula-worship:
"The true Kaulika is indeed he who performs the well-regulated observance of Kula-worship."
The mistress of the family attains union with the yoginīs and the heroes. || 2-76 ||
Even a low-born person who performs the worship of the lineage even once with devotion attains the state of the virtuous; what then need be said of the twice-born? (2.77)
Therefore, with every effort, in all circumstances and at all times, one should be devoted to the worship of the Kula for the sake of attaining one's desired fruit. (2.78)
Sacrifice is superior to family worship; vow is superior to family worship;
sacred pilgrimage site is superior to family worship; austerity is superior to family worship. (2.79)
Giving is superior to family worship; ritual action is superior to family worship;
meditation is superior to family worship; and recitation is superior to family worship. (2.80)
Greater than honoring one's family is gain; greater than honoring one's family is happiness; greater than honoring one's family is the Dharma; greater than honoring one's family is the fruit. (2-81)

Knowledge is superior through the worship of the family; the state is superior through the worship of the family; yoga is superior through the worship of the family; the goal is superior through the worship of the family. (2.82)

Fortune exceeds that of one who honors their lineage; wealth exceeds that of one who honors their lineage; learning exceeds that of one who honors their lineage; and worship exceeds that of one who honors their lineage. (2.83)
O Leader who gathers the portion of non-existence, there is no "is not," nor again "is not";
what is the use of much speaking here? O Pārvatī, hear the secret.
O Goddess, O beautiful lady, he who performs the Kula worship according to the path taught in the scriptures— near him I abide, but not by any other rule elsewhere.
"This is true, this is true, this is true; there is no doubt about it.
According to the procedure taught in the scriptures, one who knows the ritual should perform it as before. (2.86)
One should properly satisfy them with ritual objects according to the extent of one's wealth;
thus the deities become pleased and grant the fruits of all desires. (2.87)
"O Queen of the Gods, they grant the desired object of the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
Thus [is the rule for] one who performs the worship of the deity on special days. (2.88)
He who, out of Kaulika delusion, constructs the Śrīcakra according to the scriptural injunctions on our special festival days shall become dear to us both. (2.89)
"Na" means that even if one is capable, such a person becomes a beast among yoginīs—namely, that evil-minded one who creates obstacles for the Kula worship. (2.90)
In the terrible Sapātinara hell, one is tormented by twenty-one families [of beings];
therefore, with every effort, one should be devoted to the worship of the family (kulapūjā).
One attains all accomplishments; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
If one is incapable of propitiation, one should instead provide the means for worship.
He who is unable to give [a gift] should perform the act of worship and viewing;
he shall obtain the fruit that comes from properly performing a hundred sacrifices.
O beloved, by performing the sequential worship even once, one attains that fruit which one obtains by performing the sixteen great gifts (mahādāna).
By performing the sequential worship even once,
one attains that fruit which one would obtain by bathing in three and a half crores of sacred fords.
One obtains that fruit through devotion by performing the vision of the Śrīcakra;
O Goddess, what is the use of much speaking? He who gives according to his capacity [obtains the same]. (2.96)
For the sake of worshiping the family preceptor, that knower of Dharma [should provide] the family substance in the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Saura, and Sugata systems. (2.97)
O Pārvatī, [this applies] in Buddhism, the Pāśupata, Sāṃkhya, Mantra, Kālīmukha,
as well as in the Siddhānta with its right and left branches, and in the Vedic and other systems.
Any worship performed without wine and meat shall be fruitless;
one should perform recitation, worship, austerity, and vows without the substances belonging to the family [of practitioners]. (2.99)
"O Goddess, that would be fruitless, like an oblation poured into ashes. As stated in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
'The daily *śrāddha*, the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā-vandana*), and the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛ-tarpaṇa*) [are likewise essential]. (2-100)
For those who serve the family, constancy in the worship of the family is essential;
O child, one should perform the family worship without wine or meat. (2.101)
The merit of a thousand previous births is destroyed for him who indulges in liquor, meat, and sexual intercourse, even without [the prescribed] copiousness. (2.102)
One attains accomplishment through the mantra; therefore, one should be diligent in this regard.
Thus ends the praise of the Kula-worship.
Now follows the description of the worship of the Samaya.
The daily worship is the highest, while the worship on festival days is middling.
O Goddess, worship for one month is the lowest grade; beyond a month, it becomes animal sacrifice.
This is because of the failure to perform worship with the prescribed materials, such as wine and the rest, for more than a month. (2.104)
If, having become an animal, there should again arise a desire for entry [into the fold], one should initiate him once more;
[the appropriate times are] the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, as well as the new moon and the full moon. (2.105)

The transference [of consciousness] occurs on the five sacred parvans; on those meritorious days, O Īśvarī, as well as during the conjunctions of deity, lunar day, asterism, and weekday, specifically at the descent into the root of the Kula.
During lunar and solar eclipses, on the anniversaries of the Manus (manvādī), at the beginnings of the Yugas (yugādī),
upon the arrival of a spiritual teacher (deśika), and upon seeing a hero or one's own kinsmen.
On the birth-day of one's guru, on that of one's preceptor's guru, and also on the birth-day of men themselves, [one should perform] the *mānavaugha* and other rites. (2-108)

And during prosperity, recitation, gains, asceticism, initiation, vows, festivals, travel to sacred seats (pīṭha) and secondary seats (upapīṭha), and upon seeing heroes or one's own kinsmen; || 2-109 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, [this applies] when the guide is traveling for merit, upon visiting sacred fords (tīrtha) or deities, and on such occasions as these, as well as on special festival days.

In the event of diseases, calamities, great evils, or ill omens arising from bad associations, one should act according to one's strength, according to one's faith, according to one's resources, and as is appropriate. (2.111)
One should perform worship according to the time and according to the place. As stated in the *Liṅgāgama*:
"The solstice, the ninth day, the full moon, the eighth day, and the fourteenth day... (2.112).
On the Ekādaśī that coincides with the Vyatīpāta yoga, one must not allow the omission of ritual duties;
for any rite performed—whether recitation or worship—without the underlying reality is fruitless. (2.113)
Śāmbhavī becomes angry with him, and he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin at every step.
As stated in the *Tantrarāja*: "On the birthday of the Guru, as well as on the day one receives the Vidyā... (2.114).
O Lord, [I shall observe] my own birthday, as well as the day of pervasion (vyāpti),
the day of the conjunction of the three syllables, and likewise the day of the full moon.
The six joints are most excellent; [the ritual] with six, ten, or seven joints is prescribed in the *Yāmala* (p.
14): "The planting of *damanaka* is in Caitra, and the *pavitraka* rite is in Śrāvaṇa. (2-116)
In the Kulārṇava:
"O Goddess, one should have that worship of Kṛmi performed by one's own teacher or by another, or one may perform it oneself, preceded by the worship of the Vṛnda. (2-117)
One attains the world of the gods, which is free from rebirth.
One should perform daily worship by day and occasional worship at night.
"Rites for the fulfillment of desires pertain to both [the day and the night]; such is the certainty of the scripture.
O you who are worshipped by heroes, the great worship must be performed independently during the night alone. (2-119)
O lady of virtuous vows, the *nandinī* must by all means be performed according to my instruction in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*:
on a *kulavāra*, on the eighth lunar day of the *kula*, and especially on the fourteenth. (2-120)
In that context, the worship of the Yoginīs is the primary form of Kula-worship;
just as Viṣṇu, when worshipped on his own lunar day, bestows all desired objects. (2.121)
Likewise, when the lunar day (tithi) is favorable to one's family (kula), Śakti, when worshipped, grants all desires.

Regarding the characteristics of the days of the week (vāra) and so forth according to the Kula, it is stated in the Yāmala: "The Sun, the Moon, Jupiter, and Saturn—these four are remembered as being non-kula (akula). (2-122)
Mars and Venus are called "Kula"; Mercury's day is both Kula and Akula;
and the second, tenth, and sixth [tithis] are declared to be Kulākula. (2-123)
All uneven lunar days are *akula*, while the remaining ones are *kula*.
The asterisms Śatabhiṣaj, Ārdrā, Abhijit, and Mūla are declared to be both *kula* and *akula*.
Families are as numerous as the remaining *akula* portions;
when the lunar day (*tithi*), the weekday (*vāra*), and the asterism (*nakṣatra*) are situated in a *kula*, there is the light of the victorious one. (2-125)
In the Kulākhya [tradition], one is always victorious; and in the Kulākula, it is indeed gentle.
Having understood the day of the week of the Kula and so forth, the practitioner should perform the ritual action. (2.126)
Thus ends the determination of the commitments regarding the worship of the Kula.
Thus concludes the second chapter in the *Kulapradīpa* composed by the venerable Śivānandācārya.
The third chapter: now, the determination of the materials for worship.
In the *Śrīsamayācāra-tantra*, Śiva said:
"I shall now describe the materials for worship for the sake of accomplishing the desired goals of the worshipper."
Having known this correctly, the knower of mantras obtains the fruit in worship.
Liquor, meat, fish, mudrā, and sexual union—these five auspicious "M"s (makāra) are for the sake of the practice of the limbs [of yoga] and their beneficial results. (3.2)
In the Śrīkulārṇava it is also said:
"Liquor, meat, fish, parched grain, and sexual union—this group of five 'M's, O auspicious one, is the cause of delight for the deity. (3-3)
Now, the first determination of the letter *A* is in the *Samayācāra-tantra*;
in the *Śrī-rudrayāmala*,
that sacred site (*tīrtha*) is the knowledge that bestows liberation.
Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, mādhvī, and that which is produced from the grape-vine.
In the *Śrīkulārṇava*, the fivefold *vāruṇī* of the secret Wheel-King is taught as being derived from leaves,
merit, *kura*-fruit, roots, and grain-bearing fruits (3–5).
The liquor produced from juices, trees, creepers, and stalks is traditionally said to be of ten kinds;
when drunk, it fulfills one's desires and bestows supreme bliss. (3-6)
"O Beloved, this substance is appropriate and always dear; therefore, O Dear One, one should cause other non-intoxicating substances to be prepared as causes for such pride. (3.7)
Jackfruit, grapes, madhūka, dates, palm-sugar, sugarcane juice, honey-wine, sea-salt wine, mādhvīka, maireya, and coconut liquor; || 3-8 ||
These eleven are the great things that bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
but the twelfth, O beloved, is the liquor of wine, which is the most excellent of all.
Surā is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that made from honey (mādhvī).
The flour-based liquor brings about all accomplishments (siddhis), while the molasses-based liquor bestows enjoyment (bhoga).
The *mādhvī* is to be known as the bestower of liberation; the one called *surā* is dear to the deity.
Born from honey, it bestows knowledge and destroys fatal diseases. (3-11)
Mairīyī is the Mistress of the Family, and she is the remover of sins;
she is blissful and delightful, and she brings joy that is captivating to the mind. (3.12)
O Goddess, that liquor is supreme, the cause of delight for the deities;
by the mere sight of *surā*, one is liberated from all sins. (3.13)
By merely smelling its fragrance, one obtains the fruit of [offering to] Śatakratu;
by merely touching it, one obtains the fruit of visiting ten million sacred fords. (3.14)
O Goddess, from drinking that [wine], one may directly obtain the fourfold liberation.
The power of will (icchā-śakti) resides in the fragrance of the wine, while the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) resides in its taste.
And in that tasting resides the power of action (kriyā-śakti), which is established in the supreme state through its manifestation.
The white [liquor] produced from the *madirā* tree is the external means for purification. (3-16)
Having selected one among them, he should perform the rite of worship;
for an unrefined woman, through the drinking of wine, brings about quarrels, disease, and suffering. (3.17)
Well-prepared wine destroys life, fortune, fame, good luck, merit, and knowledge;
yet it removes disease, suffering, and sin. (3.18)
It increases longevity, prosperity, fame, good fortune, dharma, and knowledge; therefore, one should worship the family deity after performing the consecration according to the rules. (3.19)
Otherwise, O Dear One, the enjoyer goes to hell without a doubt; [he who] does not remember or recite [the mantra] without the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the materials.
Those great fools who remember [only this] experience suffering at every step;
for there is no mantra without liquor, and no liquor without mantra. (3.21)
"O dear one, how can there be worship when there is mutual contradiction?
Having understood that this doubt has been resolved, one should perform sacrifice according to the words of the Guru. (3.22)
When purified by inspection, sprinkling, meditation, mantra, and mudrā, the substance becomes fit for libation and a cause of delight for the deity. (3-23)
O beloved, for those people who drink the family substance (kuladravya) purified by mantra and offered by the Guru and the Deity, there is no further need to drink mother’s milk.
Just as a house enveloped in darkness is seen by means of a lamp, so too the Self, obscured by māyā, is seen through the drinking of the divine [nectar]. (3.25)
Bhairava is the deity of wine, and its power is declared to be intoxication;
even great liberated ones and wine itself can cause delusion even among the gods.
O Śivā, having drunk that maireya liquor, the man who is not transformed and remains solely intent on the midday [rite] is liberated; he is a true Kaulika.
Wine is Śakti, meat is Śiva, and he who consumes it is Bhairava himself;
the union of these two has arisen and is called bliss-liberation (ānanda-mokṣa). || 3-28 ||
Bliss is the form of Brahman, established within your body;
its manifestor is the central channel (madhya), which is therefore drunk by the yogis. (3.29)
Does this world not see Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, who carry water-pots, conchs, and skull-bowls filled with honey?
Free from apprehension, pure-minded, steady, shameless, and devoid of curiosity, one who has ascertained the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras may drink the boon-granting Varuni wine. (3.31)
O Pārvatī, through the drinking of nectar perfected by the refinement of mantra, the state of divinity arises, which liberates one from the existence of the bonds of saṃsāra. (3.32)
Wine is always forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa; for a Kṣatriya, it is forbidden at the onset of battle;
for a Vaiśya, during the plowing of cattle-pens; and for a Śūdra, during the funeral rites.
Having worshipped the gods and the ancestors according to the path taught in the divine scriptures, one who remembers the Guru while drinking liquor and eating meat incurs no fault. (3.34)
For the sake of satisfying all the gods and for the stability of meditation upon Brahman, one should consume honey and meat; yet if one consumes them out of craving, he is a sinner.
For the purpose of causing the meaning of the mantra to flash forth, for the sake of stabilizing the mind,
and for the purpose of dispelling the [obstacles] such as fear, one should practice the drinking of honey.
He who consumes liquor and other such substances for his own pleasure is a sinner;
however, one who is free from desire should consume them for the sake of pleasing the deity. (3-37)
O Dear One, the consumption of substances such as fish, meat, liquor, and so forth,
at any time other than during the occasion of a sacrifice, has not been prescribed by me.

Just as the drinking of soma by the wise during sacrifices is not considered a fault, so too should the drinking of mantra be performed at the proper time, bestowing both enjoyment and liberation. (3.39)
Having correctly understood the latent impression from the Kula scriptures of the venerable Guru, one should practice the five mudrās; otherwise, one becomes fallen. (37) (3-40)
He who worships the lineage of gurus and the Vaṭukas and others while having consumed alcohol in vain is a mere hero; he shall incur the curse of the deities. (3-41)

If a hero does not offer oblations to the god Bhairava and perform the satiation of the mantra, he will go to hell even after drinking [the wine] according to the rite for consuming the animal-sacrifice. (3.42)
Those who engage in this scripture without knowing the Kaulika conduct and without having recited the Guru’s sandals certainly cause harm to the Reality. (3.43)

For one who has fallen away from the conduct of the samaya, whose behavior is self-indulgent, and who is evil-minded, there is no attainment of siddhis; rather, there is a fall from the state of a disciple. Therefore, one should not associate with such a person. (3.44)
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims, attains neither perfection in this world nor the supreme goal in the hereafter. (3.45)
O Goddess, he who desires to consume that substance which is established in the Kaula knowledge is a great sinner, excluded from all ritual acts.

For one who acts according to their own will and is devoid of the conduct prescribed for initiation, there is no attainment of the true goal anywhere, even through pilgrimages, vows, and the like. (3.47)
One who drinks unfermented liquor, engages in sexual intercourse by force, or eats meat killed by one's own beloved shall go to the Raurava hell. (3.48)
The Kaulas stand like beasts, mocking the two eyes;
they are remembered as being ten in number, and their conduct is characterized by a state of existence in the Auras hell.
Relying on the sight of other women's wombs, he should consume the family assets; for as many times as there are grains of dust on her limbs, he is born among the sources of elemental beings. (47–50)
For one whose self is obscured by intoxication perceives nothing at all;
there is no meditation, no austerity, no worship, no dharma, and no virtuous action.
Neither the deity, nor the guru, nor the self, nor inquiry, nor the Kaula tradition [save him];
one who is merely attached to sense objects falls, without a doubt. (3.52)
One who is addicted to liquor, negligent, a meat-eater, a pursuer of women, and devoid of the Kaula instructions—he shall go to an inexhaustible hell. (3.53)
But he who, through passion, practices the five mudrās without ritual refinement, constantly attains that which is the laughter of Brahmā belonging to the Lord of the Kula. (3.54)
In the Rudrayāmala, it is said that in the Satya Yuga, one should worship with milk, ghee, honey, and flour-cakes according to the four castes;
O Goddess, in the Tretā Yuga, one should worship with ghee by all classes.
In the Tretā Yuga, one should worship her with honey and all varieties of colors; in the Kali Age, the Goddess is to be worshipped with these exclusive fermented liquors (āsava).
In the *Kulāmṛta*, in the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, and in the *Kulācāra*, one should drink the wine of Brahmā;
having drunk it otherwise out of mere desire, a man must perform an expiation. (55) 3-57
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*, O Goddess, conduct (*ācāra*) is manifold, distinguished as left (*vāma*) and right (*dakṣiṇa*).
That which is conjoined with the five mudrās and so forth is proclaimed as the left conduct. (3.58)
Devoid of the five mudrās and so forth, it is known as the Right Conduct (dakṣiṇācāra).
Listen, O Dear One, that this conduct is twofold through the division of the moist and the dry. (3.59)
One who possesses the five *makāras* is to be known as one of moist conduct (*ārdrācāra*);
one devoid of the five *makāras* is proclaimed to be of dry conduct (*śuṣkācāra*). (3.60)
O Goddess, in the Kali age, [this practice] specifically bestows the fruit of the worship of Ārdrā.
Now follows the procedure for the first consecration (*saṃskāra*) from the *Lalitāvilāsa* (3.61).
Having prepared the mud of the wings, one should arrange the worship;
on the ground in front of the left side smeared with the paste, one should draw a mandala.
Since it is taught that worship without a maṇḍala is fruitless, one should therefore draw the maṇḍala according to the rules and perform worship therein. || 3.63 ||
That which exists pervading the universe in the form of an unbroken circle, by which the three worlds are adorned—that mandala is eternally auspicious (Śiva). (3.64)
Uḍḍiyāna is square, Kāmarūpa is circular;
Jālandhara is a half-moon, and Astrapūrṇagiri is triangular. (3.65)
I shall describe the procedure for that writing as it is taught in the scriptures:
the practitioner of mantra, having sat upon a seat with his knees touching the ground, [should proceed]. (3-66)
The wise man, reciting the three *tāras* while holding his hands in the *vahatka* and *ūrdhvahasta* gestures, [should visualize] a square, a circle, a hexagon, and a triangle. (3.67)
Then, having drawn [the lines] here and there, one should draw the Kāmakalā in the center;
having thus drawn the mandala, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
Sealing with the conch-mudrā and touching [the ground] with the left hand,
one should fashion the center of the maṇḍala as a triangle by means of three lines according to the ritual procedure.
By repeating [the mantra] twice, one forms a hexagon with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and a square;
then the six seats within the hexagons are to be worshipped in order, starting from the front.
Having worshipped Uḍḍiyāṇa, Kāmarūpa, Jālandhara, and Pūrṇaśailaka, one should worship the five jewels within the four squares and other [locations].
One should worship in the four directions and in the center, proceeding clockwise; one should worship in the square enclosure with *tāra*s (the syllable Om) enclosed by *tāra*s.
Śrī, who consists of all powers, is Mahātripurasundarī (11).
[One should worship her] at the end of the word "pīṭha" with the sixty[-syllable mantra], and for the one whose nature is the fourfold [mantra]. (3.73)
One should pay homage to that great stream of the jar for the sake of the mandala;
by means of this, the wise one [should worship] the mandala with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
And having taken up the support (the vessel), it should be washed with the root-mantra three times, at the end of which [is added] the word "Śrī Mahātripura" following the Vāgbhava [syllable]. (3.75)
And for Sundarī, he established [the vessel] with the great sound, saying,
"I establish this which supports the jar," and then he established the one who bestows immortal dharma.
At the end of *prada*, at the end of *daśaśabda*, and then joined with *kalātmāṅe*, followed by *vighnyante maṇḍalāya*—this, O best of practitioners, is what has been taught. (3.77)
At the end of "Śrī Mahātripura," one should utter the word of Sundarī;
with "Namo mahāntakalaśādhārāya," one should perform worship. (3.78)
There, one should worship with perfumes and other offerings according to the sequence of the ten digits of fire:
"Huṃ huṃ! O beloved of Agni, [abiding] in the cup within the vessel of the cosmic egg. (3.79)
The mantra for the installation of the jar (kalaśa) has been proclaimed by Śiva:
at the end of Vāgbhava, "Dīpanī" is declared, followed by "Jvālāthamālinī. (3.80)
The mantra ending with the weapon [seed] preceded by the sky [letter], the sixth vowel, the crescent moon, and the *haṃsa* is declared to be the mantra for purifying the vessels. (3.81)
One should place [the mantra] into the jar with the mudrā known as the Yoni;
then, having veiled it with the Kavaca [mantra], one should subsequently place the Praṇava.
One should place there the syllables *māyā*, *hrakṣūṃ*, *haṃ*, *saṃ*, and *na* in the *na-mota* [position].
Then, taking up the jar (*kalaśa*), which has been well-worshipped with moon-fragrance, sandalwood, and other offerings— || 3.83 ||
Having uttered the word "Śrī Mahātripura" at the end of the peak-syllable (kūṭa) situated between the three stars (tritāra), and then the word "Mahākalaśa" for Sundarī; 3.84.
Having established [the object] with the thought "I place it," one then places it upon that support;

At the solar disc, preceded by *ṅe* and followed by *śrīmāhānte*, it is surrounded by *tripura*.
Having uttered the word for Sundarī, [one says] *mahākalaśaṅe namaḥ*. (3.86)
Having thus worshipped the jar, the practitioner of mantra should then meditate upon the mandala situated on the ground within it, and worship that in the same manner.
There, the digit of the Sun (Sūryakalā) is to be worshipped within a circular mandala;

Well-scented with moon-fragrance, sandalwood, musk, and jasmine,

Holding the second stream with the right hand,

To the one who bestows all desires, located at the end of the sixteen [fingers], whose nature is the Kalās;

Having cast away the defects of being seen or touched by anyone, as well as the bonds of the fettered, with the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*, he gazes with a piercing look. (3.103)

By means of that [hair], I destroy for you the sin of killing a Brahmin born from the hair;

O Goddess, may this seed-syllable *amā* be liberated from the curse of Śukra;
for if the *praṇava* is the seed of the Vedas, it consists of the bliss of Brahman. (3-112)
"By that truth, O Goddess, may you be cleansed of the slaughter of a Brahmin.
Having spoken thus, Bhārgava prostrated before the Grandfather and recited the mantras.
O Goddess, Brahmā went to his own abode;
then the purificatory rites were performed by Śambhu with Vedic mantras.
O Lakṣmī, I shall now describe that exactly as it is in the Kulārṇava Tantra:
first, Agni is extended by means of the five [verses] beginning with "svādiṣṭhayā. (3-115)
One should worship Viṣṇu with the three "yoni" verses, with the three beginning with "tvam," with the two beginning with "imaṃ me," and with the single verse beginning with "tām. (3.116)
With one [verse] for the Śoṇa [river] and one for the release from Śukra’s curse,
he should consecrate that water with these mantras, each one repeated once.
By that, the water becomes purified and is liberated from the curse of Śukra.
Then, one should write the letter *ka* conjoined with the six long vowels.
Toya (va), followed by mi, joined with kṣi; then sṛṣṭi (ṣṭi), māna (ma), āḍhya (ā), agni (ra), and asthi (sthi);

Nivṛtti is conjoined with Cakṣuḥ; this is the Svarūpa [mantra] joined with Akṣi.

The word *dīrgho* followed by *tha* alone is *vyoma*; if it is long (*dīrghāt*), then again there are two. This is the mantra *vahnijāyā*; one should also consecrate [the object] with this three times.
One should extract the sky [the letter *ha*] situated in the water [the letter *sa*], differentiated by the six long vowels.
[These are] Śrīkaṇṭheśa, Mahākāla, Recikā, and so forth, as well as Pūtanā. (3.122)
Joined with moonlight (yotsnā) are the seventh and eighth letters; Pūtanā is joined with *sadya*.
Then Nidrā, Hlādinī, Jāla, and Maṇḍikā reside [there]. (3.123)
Alternatively, the triad beginning with the seventh [letter] is water in its stable state, conjoined with fire as its protector;

Then there is Pītā, followed by Pūṣānvitā and Kākodarī with Vidhā;

The Fire [letter] joined with the left ear [v], endowed with the sharp fire [r];

Sa, Vi, Ndu, Pū, Ta, Nā, Śce, Ta, Nan, Ta, Agni, Sthāṃ, Bu, Ma, Ru, Taḥ;
again, these three [syllables] are the bones located in the pair of ears, having reached Revatī. (3-127)
The bone of Krodhīśa is for installation; Lohita is conjoined with Ananta.
Pūtanā is declared as Viśvarā, and that which is spoken by Bhṛgu is Karṇaka.
The letter *dha* should be enriched with the infinite (*ānanta*) and possess a bindu; it is joined with two *ya*s and is uneven.
Furthermore, this triad of the tortoise (*kūrma*), the wind (*pavana*), and [the others] is especially significant. (3.129)

The Sadhya-syllable accompanied by the Anvita; the Sadṛk-kūrma; the Krodhin joined with the Dīrgha; the Pavana enriched with the Bhautika and Īśa; then the Heart-mantra and the Praṇava. (65) || 3.130 ||
Māyā (H), joined with Śirāghīśa (Jha) and the bindu, followed by Bhr̥gu (Bha) possessed of the creative emission (S);
this is the Sundarī-vidyā, which releases one from curses. (3.131)

One should worship Siddhā, Raktā, Śuklā, and also Utpalā,
starting from the east and proceeding clockwise in the four directions of the square.

In the three corners, one should place the *bindu* situated in the center, conjoined with the *Kāmakalā*;
on both sides of that is *hsau*, conjoined with a *bindu*, and again behind that.
Having visualized the letter *la* together with a bindu, with the letters *sa* and *ha* on its two sides, one should there worship Ānandabhairava. (3.136)
The god has eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes; he resembles ten million suns and possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons. (3.137)
Mounted upon a bull, blue-throated, adorned with all ornaments, holding a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and sounding a bell and a ḍamaru drum. (3.138)
The meditation on the God of gods is proclaimed as follows: [one should meditate on] the red deity who holds a noose and a goad, and who bears a mace and a club. (3.139)
In his lap [he saw] the goddess Surā, whose radiance was like ten million moons,
white as gold, kunda flowers, and the moon, possessing five faces and three eyes.
Endowed with eighteen arms, with all weapons raised in her hands,
the large-eyed goddess stood laughing, facing the God of gods.

Having formed a *kūṭa* [mantra] with her name ending in the dative case, the practitioner, substituting "vaṣaṭ" for "vauṣaṭ," should worship and satisfy the Goddess. (3.146)
One should worship [the deities] surrounding the previously mentioned [central one] in the eight directions;

Liberation, the Supreme, and Time—these, together with the eight Bhairavas and the six Antakas, constitute the group of eight Bhairavas; thus, one should worship the central couple along with this group of eight.
Reciting the root mantra while gazing at that water,

The fire situated in the anus is accompanied by the *smṛti* (mind) with two eyes; it is established and conjoined with the earth element.

She is radiant as the supreme ether, the consumer of the moon, sun, and fire; she is again joined with Virajā, Smṛti, and Bhūtamālā. (3.160)
Smṛti, Bhūtamātṛ, water, Akṣi, Yuta, Ambaka;

Furthermore, these two are declared to be dear to the Fire;

Taking a drop from the *kalaśa* with one [hand], he should sprinkle it upward with the second;

Thus ends the third chapter in the *Kulapradīpa* composed by the venerable Śivānandācārya. 3.
The Fourth Chapter:
Now, the procedure for the installation of the ritual jar (kalaśa).

There, the practitioner, having sat upon his own seat, should prepare a mandala consisting of a square, a circle, a hexagon, and a triangle on his left side using the perfume known as *yakṣakardama*—composed of camphor, agallochum, musk, and *kaṅkola*—while holding a vessel of water in his two raised hands and reciting "Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ. Having drawn the *kāmakalā* in the form of a quadruple image in the center of that [mandala], he should seal that mandala with the conch-mudrā (*śaṅkhamudrā*) and, while pressing it with his left [hand], worship the center of the mandala with the root mantra, provided he is a worshiper of Śrīvidyā.

Having worshipped the triangle with three *kūṭas* and the hexagon by the repetition of two *kūṭas*, and having worshipped the triangle and hexagon starting from the eastern point and proceeding clockwise by repeating the root-mantra of the other deity; then, in the square, having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) in order—starting from the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, the center, and the four directions—if one is a worshipper of Śrīvidyā, [one should worship] in the hexagons, beginning from the eastern point: "Aṃ Āṃ Sauḥ, obeisance to Tripurā, the worthy recipient of nectar, for the sake of purification (vāsanā);
Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, obeisance to Tripureśī, whose seat is the yellow lotus."
Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ, salutation to the seat of the self of the goddess Tripurasundarī. || 4-1 ||
HAIṂ HAṂ KLĪṂ HSAUṂḤ: Salutation to Tripuravālinī, who possesses three and a half faces.
HSAIṂ HRĪṂ KLĪṂ HSAUṂ: Salutation to Tripurā Śrī, the seat of all mantras. || 4-2 ||

*Hrīṃ klīṃ vlūṃ*, obeisance to Tripuramālinī, the seat of accomplishment for the object of practice (*sādhya*). Having thus worshipped the six seats, one should worship the square, the circle, the hexagon, and the triangle with: "Obeisance to Kāmarūpa-pīṭha."
Salutation to Jālandhara-pīṭha.
Salutation to Pūrṇagiri-pīṭha.
Homage to Uḍḍiyāna-pīṭha.

Having thus worshipped the four seats, one should worship in a clockwise direction within the square—at the four cardinal directions starting from the front and in the center—with the mantra: *glūṃ gaganaratnāya namaḥ*.
Slūṃ, salutation to the jewel of heaven.
mlūṃ, obeisance to the jewel among mortals.
Plūṃ, obeisance to the jewel of the netherworld (pātāla).
Nlūṃ, obeisance to the Nāga-ratna.

Having thus worshipped the five jewels, one then [recites]: "Obeisance to the Maṇḍala, which is the support of the Great Vase (mahākalaśa) consisting of the four seats (pīṭha), and which is the root of the Śrī Paradevatā who embodies all powers."

Having thus worshipped the entire maṇḍala, one should place the base (ādhāra) washed with the root mantra, thinking: "I establish the base for the great jar of the Śrī Paradevatā. Having established it, one worships it with: "Obeisance to the Fire-maṇḍala, which consists of ten kalās that bestow dharma, and serves as the base for the great jar of the Śrī Paradevatā. Then, having invoked the [kalās] beginning with Dhūmrārcis upon it, saying: "O you whose essence is the ten kalās beginning with Dhūmrārcis, come here!
one says: "Yaṃ, obeisance to Dhūmrārcis."
Ra, for Uṣmā.
Laṃ to Jvalinī.
Vaṃ, to Jvālinī.
Śaṃ, obeisance to Visphuliṅginī.
Oṃ Saṃ, obeisance to Suśrī;
Oṃ Saṃ, obeisance to Svarūpā.
Haṃ, obeisance to Kapilā.
Laṃ to Havyavāhā.
KṢAṂ, obeisance to Kavyavāhā.

Having thus worshipped the ten digits (kalās), one should then [worship] the pitcher made of gold or other materials and perfumed with incense, reciting: "Haṃ Ha! To the goblet of the Cosmic Egg, Svāhā!"

Thus, having washed [the vessel] with the left hand, one should inflame it with the Sandīpinī Vidyā using the Āyoni-mudrā while reciting: *Aiṃ Saṃdīpini Jvālāmālinī Hrīṃ*. It should be veiled with the Kavaca-mantra: *Oṃ Namaḥ Hna Kṣūṃ Namaḥ Haṃ Namaḥ Saṃ Namaḥ*, which are the mantras for the five mudrās applied therein. Then, having established the great jar (*kalaśa*) there with the mantra: *Oṃ I Śrīmahātripurasundaryā Mahākalaśaṃ Sthāpayāmi* (I establish the great jar of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī), one should then offer salutation to the sun-disk with the mantra:

*Aṃ Haṃ Arthapradaṃ Dvādaśakalātmane Arkamaṇḍalāya Śrīparadevatāyāmā Kalashāya Namaḥ* (Salutation to the Sun-disk, the bestower of wealth, consisting of twelve kalās, the mother of the Śrī Supreme Deity, and the jar).

Having thus worshipped within the pitcher, one should visualize the previously mentioned maṇḍala there, worship the five jewels as before, and then invoke the twelve kalās of the Sun into that [maṇḍala].
Kaṃ bhaṃ, salutation to Tāpinī.
Khaṃ vaṃ, salutation to Tāpinī. Gaṃ kaṃ, salutation to Dhūmrā.
Ghaṃ maṃ, salutation to Marīcī; Ṅaṃ naṃ, salutation to Jvālinī;
Chaṃ daṃ, salutation to Suṣumṇā.
Jaṃ dhaṃ, obeisance to Bhogadā; jhaṃ taṃ, obeisance to Viśvā;
jaṃ ṇaṃ, obeisance to Vodhinī.
*Ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ*, obeisance to Dhāriṇī;
*Ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ*, obeisance to Kṣamā.

Having thus worshipped, one should then worship once the *Tīrthadhāman* (the vessel of sacred water), which is covered with red cloth and adorned with red garlands. Then, using that *tīrtha* held in the right hand—scented with moon-plant (*candana*), sandalwood, musk, and flowers, and flowing from a stream untouched by the second [finger]—while reciting the root mantra and the *mātṛkā* in reverse order, one should fill the jar of the Śrī Paradevatā with the words: "I fill the jar of the Śrī Paradevatā. Obeisance to the nectar of the jar of the Śrī Paradevatā, who previously was *uṃ saṃ*, the soul of the sixteen digits that bestows desires."

Having thus worshipped the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one should place a *māṣa*-weight of meat and fish therein, recite the root mantra, stir that sacred ford with a flower, and cast that flower outside. Then, having recited "klīṃ," one should place red flowers mixed with the eight fragrances (*aṣṭagandha*) there, and having looked upon them with the *gālanī-mudrā* while reciting "sauḥ," one should worship the previously mentioned mandala in the sacred ford according to the previously stated method, and invoke the lunar digits (*somakalā*) therein.
Aṃ, obeisance to Amṛtā; Āṃ, obeisance to Mānadā;
Iṃ, obeisance to Pūṣā.
Īṃ, obeisance to Tuṣṭi; Uṃ, obeisance to Puṣṭi;
Ūṃ, obeisance to Rati.
Ṛṃ, salutation to Dhṛti;
Ṝṃ, salutation to Śaśinī;
Ḷṃ, salutation to Candrikā.
Ḷṃ, salutation to Kānti;
eṃ, salutation to Jyotsnā; ai, salutation to Śrī.
Oṃ, obeisance to Prīti. Auṃ, obeisance to Aṅgadā. Aṃ, obeisance to Pūrṇā.
"Aḥ, obeisance to Pūrṇāmṛtā.
Thus one worships around that square.
"Oṃ īṃ ha sa kha phreṃ, obeisance to the deities of the pathways, huṃ phaṭ svāhā."
Hasakhaphreṃ grāmacaṇḍālinī huṃ phaṭ svāhā namaḥ! Hasakhaphreṃ krodhacaṇḍālinī huṃ phaṭ svāhā namaḥ! Hasakhaphreṃ dṛṣṭicaṇḍālinī huṃ phaṭ svāhā namaḥ!
Hasakhaphreṃ, [the mantra] for touching, Caṇḍī. Hasakhaphreṃ, [the mantra] for creation, Caṇḍī.
Hasakhaphreṃ ghaṃ yaṃ caṃ, Hasakhaphreṃ, [the mantra] for the evil of being seen or touched by all people, Caṇḍī.

Having worshipped [the deity] by circumambulating clockwise with the mantra *hasakhaphre paśupāśa caṃ*, and having cast away the ten defects, one should worship in the center with the mantra: *oṃ kāṃ kīṃ kūṃ kaiṃ kauṃ kaḥ vikāraśoṣiṇi asya vikārān han han svāhā*.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman, eternal and composed of both the gross and the subtle;
by means of it, I pacify the sin of killing a Brahmin born from the *kaca* [portion of the Veda].
O you who are born from the solar disc, O you who arise from the abode of Varuṇa!
O Goddess, who consists of the seed-syllable *Am*, may [this one] be liberated from the curse of Śukra.
If the *praṇava* is the seed-syllable of the Vedas and is composed of the bliss of Brahman,
by that truth, O Goddess, may you dispel the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having consecrated [the substance] with these mantras: *Hvāṃ hvīṃ hvūṃ hvaiṃ hvauṃ hvaḥ, amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛteśvari amṛtavarṣaṇi amṛtaṃ srāvaya 2, śukraśāpāt sudhāṃ mocaya 2, mocikāyai namaḥ;
oṃ jūṃ saḥ svāhā*—having thus consecrated it eight times with this vidyā, then [recite]: *Oṃ śāṃ śīṃ śūṃ śaiṃ śauṃ śaḥ, śāpaṃ vimoci sā vai surāṃ devyai namaḥ*.

Having thus consecrated [the vessel] three times, then [recite]: *oṃ klīṃ śrīṃ krīṃ śrīṃ krūṃ kraiṃ krauṃ kraḥ, release the curse of Surekṛṣṇa, cause the nectar to flow, cause it to flow, svāhā*. Flow forth as the first leader of the sweet juices; flow toward the great gods with exhilarating food.

Having consecrated it three times with the mantra: "O Bhūta, manifest the vibration of consciousness (citsphuraṇa) even in the form of the supreme nectar," and then having consecrated it five times with the Dīpinī Vidyā: "Aiṃ vada vada vāgvādini, Aiṃ klīṃ klinne kledini kledaya kledaya mahākṣobhaṃ kuru kuru klīṃ sauḥ mokṣaṃ kuru 2 klīṃ sauḥ mokṣaṃ kuru 2 sauḥ hsauḥ," one then recites:

Thus, having worshipped and gratified the nine Bhairavas in the center and in the eight directions, one should gaze at [the water] with the *mūlavidyā* while forming the *vīkṣaṇa-mudrā*; sprinkle it with the *astra-mantra*; strike it three times with *kuśa* grass empowered by the *astra-mantra*; sprinkle it again with the *kavaca-mantra*; and offer the *arghya*. Aiṃ vada vada klīṃ vāgvādinī sauḥ svāhā. || 4-15 ||

From these two, that best of jewels begot a daughter who was dark-complexioned,

She is endowed with wisdom, holding a śārikā bird and a rosary in her lotus-like hands; she has large eyes and is adorned with a conch-shell earring.

then the goddess became renowned as Mātaṅgī, the bestower of boons.

performed the worship of the womb (yoni-pūjā) with passion within the Triple City (Tripurajña).

then the wicked king, becoming enraged, seized his beloved by the hair.
From that time forward, during the enchanting Dūtī-yāga,
Śambhu, accompanied by her, would engage in sexual union while reciting the Praṇava.
The mantra named Mātaṅgī, which had emerged from within the Praṇava and generates all prosperity, then became a garland.
With words full of aesthetic flavor, he spoke to the Goddess an irreproachable discourse that delights the world,
concerning the mantra of Mātaṅgī, which intensely brings about the arousal of passion.
That goddess, being afflicted by emptiness, is therefore known as Antyajā;
situated among the lowest castes, Mātaṅgī then becomes Antyajā.
She established a unity between the lowest castes and the twice-born, which is highly praised;
that Goddess, having then granted a boon to all the social orders, bestowed that excellent gift.
No fault is to be recognized therein; all of that has been enjoined by the Śruti.
That which was performed for the sake of the Goddess's liberation is devoid of defect.
This scripture is divine and not to be spoken; it is enjoined by the Vedas.

This must be guarded with effort and never spoken in the presence of the uninitiated;
O fortunate one, have no doubt, for this truth has been spoken by me. (6.69)

In the worship of Mātaṅgī, which is most excellent during the captivating sacrifice of the messenger (dūtī), a worship performed without the worship of the womb (yonipūjā) becomes as if it were not performed at all. (6–70)
By remembering him, anyone may become omniscient and free from all afflictions; such a person attains immeasurable longevity, health, and prosperity. (6.71)
