The washerwoman, the leather-worker, the outcaste woman, the excellent housewife, the celebrated courtesan, and the enchanting woman joined with the mantra are [the best] for worship. (6.82)
If Mātaṅgī were a courtesan, then even that courtesan was in her menses;
and when she was in her menses, she was considered the most excellent of all. (6.83)
Likewise, in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*: "The messenger (dūtī), having cast aside all fear and shame, should then place [the consort], who is endowed with youthful exuberance, upon the couch. (6.84)
Having cast aside her skull-cup as well as her garment, O Pārvatī, she becomes a devoted follower of the Teacher, delighting him with her mind. (6.85)
O beloved, having abandoned the state of a physical body, those whose arms are closely entwined engage in kissing,
embracing, and the scratching of nails and teeth.
What is the use of saying more here? One should practice the unification with the vital breath (prāṇa).
He whose female messenger (dūtī) is well-known is one whose life is fruitful. (6.87)
Having uplifted both lineages, one attains the eternal state;
one obtains perpetual happiness and gains all sovereign power. (6.88)
For him there shall be no misfortune whatsoever, nor shall there be any fear of death; by kissing he attains supreme sovereignty, and through the wounds of nails and teeth, he gains long life.
And one should bestow the bliss of union, for that is Viṣṇu’s supreme state;
he who does not grant a kiss will certainly become poor.
O Goddess Pārvatī, without embracing [her], one becomes afflicted with leprosy;
O Goddess, in this world, one who has been bitten by a forest-dweller [or bitten by a wild animal] becomes censured.
But by giving it for the fifth time, she becomes the virtuous Sāvitrī;
in the second [giving] she would not be Lakṣmī, but in the third she becomes Pārvatī.
From that, one should grant her an abundance of happiness; her merit is beyond calculation.
Through an embrace, she removes diseases; through a kiss, she bestows wealth, grain, and the like.
Through nail-marks, tooth-wounds, and the like, liberation is then produced;
she will not be joined in union—that is the truth, there is no doubt. (6.94)
In the *Uttaratantro*:
"When only one watch of the night has passed, the man should then go to the house of the Kula woman, his mouth filled with betel and fragrant with the scent of incense. (6.95)
With his limbs smeared with red sandalwood, wearing red garlands and unguents,
and clad in red garments, he stands in a house as crimson as lac.
Clad in red garlands and adorned with red flowers, one should worship the Mistress of the Kula through the conventions of the five causes. (6.97)
Nor [should one accept food from] an actress, a palanquin-bearer, a prostitute, a woman of the Pulkasa caste, a washerwoman, a dyer, a maidservant, or a newly married woman. (6.98)
The chalk-maker, the potter, as well as the cowherd’s daughter—
all these women of noble family are especially endowed with the power of burning.
Devoted solely to the guru, free from compassion and shame, intent on concealment—such young women generally bestow all accomplishments. (6.100)
One should bring some of these brushes for him who would worship [the deity], provided she is endowed with the practice of non-duality, devoted to the guru, and firm in her vows. (6.101)
One who is constantly devoted to practice, endowed with sattvic devotion, free from the turbidity of envy, of noble birth, and affectionate toward her devotees. (6.102)
Endowed with cleverness and magnanimity, possessed of virtues such as courtesy,
and endowed with beauty and youth, she was distinguished by her character and good fortune.
Whether she has been previously taken as a wife or has come for a tryst,
she is smeared with red perfume and adorned with red garments.
One should employ a slender female messenger who possesses fragrant red flowers, is adorned with all ornaments, and has been well-perfumed with incense for the performance of the rite.
One should worship her thus situated upon a couch of flowers, having bathed, wearing clean linen garments and the like, and adorned with ointments. (6.106)
Having seated her, whose limbs were adorned yet weary, with a welcome and a seat,
he placed her upon a mattress in the center, covered with fragrant flowers.
Upon one's own couch, strewn with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, saffron, and other such substances, one should worship the Mistress of the Kula.

Having performed the placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement on the hands (karanyāsa), and thereafter the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the Mātṛkānyāsa and then place [the mantras] upon the limbs of the Kula.
Then, having performed the placement of the vessel for the *arghya* offering and so forth according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should worship the Mistress of the Kula in the center of the couch.
One should also worship Maṇḍūka in the center of the couch, and in front of him,
Kālāgnirudra, Ādhāraśakti, Kūrma, and Ananta.
One should worship the Boar, the Earth, the bulb, the lotus stalk, the filaments, the lotus flower, the pericarp, and the mandala.
One should worship Dharma, dispassion, sovereignty, knowledge, as well as ignorance, lack of sovereignty, lack of dispassion, and even Adharma. (6.113)
One should also worship the Jñānātman, the Jīvātman, and the Paramātman;
having offered scents, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth, one should perform the worship right there.
Having placed the mandala upon it and performed the ritual worship,
one should then, with a concentrated mind, worship the five objects of desire within that [mandala].
Hrīṃ is indeed Kāmarāja, Klīṃ is Kaṃdarpa, Aiṃ is Manmatha, Blū is Mīnaketana, and Strī is indeed Manobhava. (6.116)
Having worshipped with flowers joined with fragrance preceded by "Oṃ" and ending with "namaḥ" and "ṅe taṃ," one should worship the Mistress of the Kula in the four directions.
[One should worship] Baṭuka, Bhairava, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla.
In another Tantra, [the mantras are] Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, and the Strībīja (which is also Kāmarāja). (6.118)
Having offered the *hasavlermantra*, one should then utter the *ādhāraśakti*;
then, having offered the *śrīpādukā*, one should say, "I worship; [I offer] *namaḥ*."
O fair-faced one, having inscribed a beautiful triangle there on her forehead with this mantra using vermilion and other substances, || 6.120 ||
In the Uttaratantra:

"Having drawn a triangular yantra upon her head, the practitioner [should place] Gaṇeśa on the crown of the head, the Lord of the Kula at the tips of the hair, and [the deity] on the forehead. (6.121)
One should worship Durgā on the two feet, Lakṣmī on the tongue, Sarasvatī on the two breasts, and Madana residing within the two breasts as well. || 6.122 ||
Having placed the moon (the syllable *sa*) in the mouth and the seed-syllable *hūṃ* uttered immediately thereafter at the back,
one should take refuge in the southern direction from head to foot.
One should worship the digits of Kāma within all the limbs of that [consort]:
faith, love, passion, fortitude, fame, and the mind-born [desire]. (6.124)
Vimalāmodinī, Ghorā, Madanonmādinī, as well as Mohidīpinī, Śodhinī, and Śāṅkarī.
And Rañjinī, as well as Madanā and Kalāsvaravirājitā—
there, the Moon-phases (Candrakalās) are to be worshipped from the head down to the feet.
Pūṣā, Vaśā, Sumanas, Rati, Prīti, Dhṛti, Krūdhī, Saumyā, Amarīcī, and likewise Caṇḍamālinī.
Aṅgirā, Śaśinī, Chāyā, as well as Saṃpūrṇamaṇḍala, Tuṣṭi, and Amṛtā— these lunar digits (candrakalās) are to be worshipped.
Indeed, she should be worshipped with the very vowels for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals. As stated in the *Lalitāvyāptidīpikā*:
"In her womb, there exist three principal channels. (129)
One nāḍikā belongs to the Moon, another nāḍikā belongs to the Sun, one belongs to Agni, and another is beyond being known; the practitioner should worship them.
The lunar [digit] flows as water, the solar [digit] flows as flowers, and the one known as Aṇimā flows as seed; one should worship them by their respective names.
With a well-pleased mind, one should worship [the deities] using the [syllables] beginning with Vāgbhava joined with "namas";
according to the Uttaratantra,
one should worship in the chamber of Madana, which has been smeared with red sandalwood paste.
Having uttered the Bhagamālā mantra, one should worship after the three Tārās;
then, having extracted "ai hrīḥ śrīḥ ai," followed by "vlūṃ vlūṃ klinne. (133)
"Bring all things under my control!"—having thus [uttered this], [one should worship].

Then, having worshipped that wheel with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), [one should recite]: "strīṃ hrīṃ blūṃ klīṃ, obeisance and svāhā to Bhagamālinī, the one who is moist. || 6-134 ||
Having worshipped her with incense, lamps, and various food offerings, the practitioner of the lineage should bow to her and himself partake of the remains of the offering (ucchiṣṭa).
Immediately thereafter, one should worship [the deity] on one's own head with incense, perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
then the root mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ śivāya*. (136)
One should utter the Aghora and Sadyojāta mantras, as well as Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and immediately after that, Vidyā. (137)
Then, after reciting Śānti, Śāntitīrthā, and the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga),
one should utter the entire vidyā and worship the triangle.
Then, having obtained his permission and offered him excellent betel,
he placed Śiva there with the mudrā known as Gajatuṇḍa.
One should recite the mantra "Dharmādharma" eight thousand times;
having vomited in the morning, one should discard the principle known as Prakāśa according to the sage's instruction.
"O Manu, wherever the union of Śiva and Śakti arises, there both [aspects] are to be grasped, such as dharma and adharma."
One should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, or even one hundred and eight times, free from agitation, with a steady mind and undisturbed. (142)
That which has been recited as japa should immediately thereafter be offered to the Goddess;
then, with his face [turned toward] the blissful Bhava, he may sport happily for a long time. 143.
Therefore, the seeker should take the liquid of the moon from the skull (galacca) and that born of the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*;
he should then apply these to the vessel for the *arghya*, the yantra, and the sandalwood paste. || 144 ||
This mudrā, known as Gajatuṇḍā, bestows the desired objects of the mind;
it is the supreme of the supreme nectar of Kuṇḍodbhavā in the Devīyāmala, O Goddess. (145)
Among those, the first is the power of darkness (tamas), the middle is pure passion (rajas) alone,
the lowest is human power, and another is even lower than the lowest.
In the Rudrayāmala:
Furthermore, any man who, out of malice or even out of greed, acts as a mantra-practitioner regarding the source of the Liṅga, shall go to the Raurava hell. (147)
Thus ends the sacrifice to the messenger (dūtī-yāga).
Now follows the procedure for taking the kuṇḍa, gola, and so forth,
on the fifth lunar day of the impurity (mala).
Then, having offered cavya as a relish for sucking, as well as garments, ornaments, and so forth,
one should worship her with pure, unblinking eyes in that temple of Madana.
One should meditate upon them with a passionate disposition and not abandon their true nature;
for one who possesses pure mantras and medicinal herbs, one should not churn the abode of passion.
Furthermore, as she is being churned, that supreme reality arises;
one should diligently take up that auspicious substance born from the vessel (kuṇḍa). 150.
The *mathana* [mudrā] is performed with the *gajahasta* (elephant-trunk) gesture.
In the Śaktiyāmala: "I shall enter the self-existent [liṅga] for the sake of the worship of the practitioner;
having brought a divine woman, intoxicated and exalted by youth. (6.151)
[He should initiate] one who has been consecrated with the root mantra, who has a beautiful nose, a lovely smile, a heart always filled with bliss, and who is devoid of pity and shame. (6.152)
O beautiful goddess, one should cause her— who is devoted to the guru, well-attired, and intent on the worship of the deity—
to perform the placement of the phonemes (nyāsavarṇa) as before.
In her temple of passion, the practitioner, having himself become intent upon liberation, should worship the Supreme Goddess on the fifth lunar day.
O Sovereign Goddess of the Gods, you are the power whose will is sovereign and who is manifest as the Goddess herself;
therefore, that which is her own flower must be protected with great effort. (6.155)
One should always worship Śakti with garments, ornaments, and flowers;
according to the season and according to whatever flower has fallen of its own accord. (6.156)
Having taken that *svayambhū* flower with great care, one should perform [the rite].
In the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*:
"Listen to the supremely auspicious majesty of all the substances belonging to the family. (6.157)
Whatever great desire is obtained by reaching one's family deity,
that [is attained] on the new moon day when the Goddess resides within the Suṣumṇā.
She indeed rains down nectar upon the surface of the earth for three days;
on that lunar day, having observed one's own lineage, if one should recite the vidyā. (6.159)
For indeed, every accomplishment shall arise there with each and every recitation;
therefore, with every effort, examine the *kula* and perform the recitation. (6.160)
Having seen that nectar, O God, and having taken up what has flowed down,
one should accomplish every practice for the sake of attaining the Kula conduct.
When Śakti is devoid of Śiva, she indeed rains that down at the beginning;
at that very time, there is the supreme, divine [substance] known as Svayaṃbhukusuma.
The substance known as *svayaṃbhukusuma* is difficult to obtain even throughout the three worlds;
O Lord, it may perhaps be found here and there by the King of the Gandharvas.
O Lord, when it is obtained, one should mix it with lac juice;
having made a pill by adding musk and saffron, one should then conceal it. (6.164)
If the practitioner, having drawn the King of Yantras, should worship it with this application of unbroken rice, he shall attain great accomplishment. (6.165)
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
"Listen to the fifth secret for the bathing of the deities, by which, O Goddess, when the bath is performed, the deities become pleased. (6.166)
At night, during the fifth period, having performed the supreme fifth [rite],
one should diligently take whatever substance is found within the bhaga.
The water produced from that pool should be known as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is obtained through the conjunction of good fortune and is difficult even for the gods to attain. (6.168)
Having poured a little water into that [substance], one should hold it in a copper vessel;
by the mere act of bathing with that substance, the deities become pleased. (6.169)
O Aśubhagā, one should take that first menstrual blood of women which arises at a particular age, for it is difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to obtain. (6.170)
O Goddess, if by the power of fortune one obtains this flower called *svayaṃbhūkusuma* for the delight of the deities— (6.171)
Then, O fair-faced one, the practitioner of mantra should perform the supreme bath for his own deities;
he shall obtain his desired object—this is the truth, the absolute truth. (6.172)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) using the mantra bestowed by one's own guru;
thereafter, one should cause the fifth [limb] to be performed upon the body of the Śakti or upon one's own body.
Then one should perform recitation and other rites, and one obtains inexhaustible fruit;
this secret has been told for the purpose of bathing the deity. (6.174)
This secret has been declared in the tantras of the six traditions;
one should perform it especially in the tantras of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya). || 175 ||
O beloved, for women whose husbands are living, one should have the fifth [rite] performed;
whatever substance belongs to her vulva (bhaga), that is considered to be produced from a cow-tail (golodbhava).
O beautiful lady, listen now to what should be done in the absence of substances produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*:
how one should perform the ritual bath for the sake of pleasing the deity. (6.177)
Having taken the flower of whichever tree it may be with great care,
one should then cast it into water that has been rubbed with red sandalwood.
With that water, one should perform the supreme bathing of the deity;
one obtains the desired fruit—this is the truth, the truth, O fair-faced one. (6.179)
In the Rudrayāmala:
"O Queen of the Gods, you are not satiated even by thousands of jars or hundreds of loads of water at a sacred ford, without the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga. (6.180)

The vulva is the sacrificial ladle, the phallus is the bolt, and the sprout of the vulva is the clarified butter; [the seed] is the potency and the mind is the Hotṛ priest—thus it is stated in the Bhairava Āgama. (6.181)
Having summoned the female messengers and taken up the supreme reality,
and having placed it in the vessel of the *āli*, one should then perform the worship.
Thus ends the procedure for taking the substances such as *kuṇḍagola* and so forth.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Kulapradīpa composed by the venerable Gosvāmin Śivānanda.
The Seventh Chapter: An Exposition of the Kula Conduct, from the Śrī Kulārṇava.

Accompanied by worship and consecration, knowing the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, devoted to the deity and the guru, self-restrained, and fond of ritual worship—such a one is dear [to me]. (7.1)
O Mistress of the Kula, one who knows the secrets of the family lineage, who is eager to propitiate the deity, and who is endowed with the instructions of the guru, should perform worship. (7.2)
May he not be without grace, being united with the power of Rudra;
thereafter, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with the substances proclaimed by Śrī Bharava.
Otherwise, by failing to follow the method of the guru’s instruction, one will fall;
O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the worship of the Śrīcakra through the yoga of mantra.
Therefore, knowing "I am Bhairava," and realizing "I am omniscient and endowed with all virtues," I myself shall respectfully accept [this] together with you. (7.5)
Having reflected thus, the lord of yogis should perform the family worship (kulapūjā).
Endowed with such characteristics as these, he is a Kaulika who observes the fixed vow. (7.6)
O Goddess, he who worships her with offerings that are spoiled, stale, leftover, foul-smelling, or devoid of fragrance shall attain the enjoyment of worldly prosperity and liberation.
Satisfying [the ancestors] with substances that have been placed in another vessel, even if they are most delicious, intoxicating, and produced from nectar, shall be fruitless. (7–8)
O Maheśānī, through these captivating [offerings], the libation becomes fruitful;
[the Guru should offer it] to his own Śakti or another Śakti who has been initiated and is foremost among disciples.
"Even after having them drink the *vedadravya*, O Ambikā, one should immediately perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) for women who have not been initiated," so it was spoken by Śaṅkara.
One who knows the ritual procedure for mantra-initiation becomes pure, and not otherwise.
Therefore, [one should worship] a Śakti possessing auspicious marks with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and so forth.
Having worshipped the deity with his intellect, he should offer the vessel of enjoyments;
at the end of that, he should also offer young maidens and captivating women.
Having worshipped the deity with the intellect, one should offer the vessel individually for each.
But he who, being capable, partakes of the family substance (kuladravya) without having first offered it [to the deity]—|| 7.13 ||
That worship should be known as fruitless; the deity is not pleased.
One should perform worship together with heroes who are endowed with the true tradition. (7.14)
Having performed mutual salutations, one should drink with their permission;
having lifted the vessel with the left hand and formed the mudrā with the right (apasavya).
O Mistress of the Kula, one should receive it according to the rite by uttering the mantra before the venerable Guru and the elders. (7.16)
"One should not drink a substance while seated"—this is the firm conclusion of the scripture.
One should not drink a substance without the mantra; for doing so, an expiation is prescribed. (7.17)
Therefore, O Mistress of the Family, it should be performed according to the ritual of the mantra:
"I drink this pure nectar; may you be my medicine. (7-18)
The cause for the total severance of the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa) has been proclaimed by Bhairava;
for in that state, the mind’s own sovereignty is its essence, and because of that, it consists of bliss. (7.19)

Because all things consist of that [consciousness] and because the essence of things is withdrawn, their own inherent flavor is drunk by themselves for the sake of unfolding their own sovereignty. (7.20)
Therefore, O Goddess of the gods, the knower of mantras drinks this goddess Surā, who is Pūrṇādūtā, with this root mantra. (7.21)
One who has not drunk the liquor should perform the measurement calmly and very slowly;
at the end of the meal is the poisonous substance, and at the end of the substance is the poisonous meal.
One should know that to be nectar which is food together with wine;
O beloved, drinking accompanied by chewing is declared to be nectar. (7.23)
Drinking without chewing merely increases the poison;
drinking is said to be of three kinds according to the sequences of the hero (vīra), the animal (paśu), and the other [the divya].

The divine drink is prescribed for before the Goddess; the heroic drink is prescribed for the dismissal [of the deities]. That which is drunk according to one's own will like an animal is called the animal-drink (paśupāna). (7.25)
The divine drink bestows enjoyment and liberation, while the drink for the heroes bestows liberation;
the drink for the animal-like [uninitiated] leads to hell—such shall be the fruit of drinking. (7.26)
As long as there is no wavering or delusion in one's view, mind, speech, and body, so long should one practice drinking; beyond this is the drinking of the Paśu.
O Indra, as long as the ritual procedure (kalpa) is not yet complete, and as long as the face of the vessel is not turned upward, one may drink the substance; otherwise, one would go to hell. (7.28)
O Goddess, for those who are endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), drinking [the nectar] is prescribed;
having lifted the vessel with both hands, one should remember the Root Mantra and the Pādukā mantra. (7.29)
One should drink wine until the throat is filled; there is no doubt that one is liberated thereby.
Drinking again and again, drinking repeatedly, until one falls to the ground. (7.30)
Having risen and drunk again, rebirth no longer exists.
From bliss the Goddess is inflamed; from fainting, Bhairava himself [is inflamed]. (7.31)
Because of vomiting [the impurities], all the gods [are pleased]; therefore, one should perform this triad.
Indeed, that is the bliss of the Kula-yogins who are devoted to the divine drink (divyapāna).
Even the happiness of a sovereign monarch is not equal to that bliss which belongs to those devoted to their lineage who partake of the ancestral heritage. (7.33)
O fair-faced one, that very bliss would indeed be liberation; this is the truth.
[The stages of life are] the infant, the young, the adolescent, and the mature. (7.34)
And at its end is the seventh, the Radiance of Youth (taruṇollāsa).
O Mistress of the Kula, beginning from that, the triad of principles (tattvatraya) has been declared.
O Ambikā, the Radiance of Youth has been described; "youth" refers to the face.
O beloved, youth is said to be the perfect blossoming of the mind; when there is stumbling in the eyes, face, and speech, it is designated as "mature. (7.36)
One who desires the union of vessels (*pātramelana*) in the supreme wheel (*pare cakre*) should never perform it prior to the full blossoming of maturity (*prauḍhasamullāsa*).
In that case as well, one should perform the "fusion of vessels" (pātramelana) according to one's qualification,
[avoiding] those who are uninitiated, of improper conduct, ignorant of the truth, and devoid of the deity.
One should not associate with those who corrupt others and have fallen from their commitments;
rather, one should associate with those who know the words, sentences, and means of valid cognition, and who understand the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti. (7.39)
O beloved, if one is ignorant of the family traditions, one should avoid such attachment;
even if born into a noble family, those who are aged and abide by their own proper conduct [should be followed]. (7-40)
O beloved Pārvatī, if they should become averse to your worship, one should avoid their company—even that of one's wife, sons, friends, and kinsmen, however affectionate they may be. (7.41)
O beloved, one should avoid the company of those who are ignorant of family traditions, as well as those who have never seen men and those who dwell in foreign lands. (7.42)
Without the application of the secret convention (saṃketa), one should not perform the union of substances;
nor should one share a single vessel, even if one is the Lord of the Kula himself. (7.43)
The mantras turn away and obstacles arise at every step;
furthermore, one should not offer the substance contained in one's own vessel to Bhairava.
O Maheśānī, if one were to give [these things], the deity would incur a curse;
[namely] the seat, food, vessel, clothing, bed, and so forth. (7.45)
One should never cause Śaṅkara to be performed by those who lack direct realization or who are unworthy;
rather, [the offering] should be the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) bestowed by yogins and yoginīs.
O Dear One, one should drink [the nectar] from which the sandals of one's mother have been removed, over which the root mantra has been recited;
or, if at any time a vessel of honey is obtained by chance, one should drink it with devotion.

Having taken [it] as before and having recited [the mantra], O Goddess, one should drink it while remembering the Guru, as well as the Guru’s Śakti and sons, and the Guru’s elder and younger brothers. (7.48)
O Pārvatī, one may eat the leavings even of one's own elder brother, but not those of anyone else;
one should drink the substance that is the leavings of the Śakti, and chew the leavings of the Vīra.
One should not give one's own leavings, nor should one eat the leavings of others.
One may eat the leavings of women, but one should not offer one's leavings to them. (7.50)
O Goddess of the gods, otherwise there would be a fall from the center of the wheel;
one should give the remains of one's own food to one's youngest disciples, O Ambikā.

If one should give [food] out of affection to others, he would become a vessel for calamities; likewise, the foolish-minded person who takes a vessel that has not been cleared of remnants [incurs the same]. (7.52)
Out of affection, greed, or even fear, a deity may incur a curse; the practice of performing one's own desired actions is proclaimed as "mature internal [conduct]. (7.53)
O Goddess, when the circle of yoga has rejoiced in the radiance of the mature culmination, and likewise in the circle of the Yoginīs, the wheel is said to be bliss. (7.54)
"When the heroes have taken root, no further task remains to be done;
this very mastery of the scriptures is the command of the Supreme Lord. (7.55)
In that regard, whatever action is performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
all of it arises for the pleasure of the deity, O beautiful goddess.
Idle chatter is the fruit of recitation; drowsiness is said to be meditative absorption (samādhi).
O Goddess, physical transformation is worship, and vomiting is the offering (bali) to Bhairava.
Liberation is the union with power; praise is speaking at that time;
ritual placement (nyāsa) is the touching of the limbs; and the act of oblation is performed with ladles.
O Īśānī, looking [at the Guru] is meditation, and lying down is prostration;
whatever movement there is for one who is single-mindedly absorbed in that bliss is itself a virtuous rite.
But he who deliberates upon what should and should not be done becomes a sinner;
for the heroes and the yoginīs residing in this wheel are slow with intoxication.
O Goddess of the gods, they act according to their mental inclination and enthusiasm; forgetting what they themselves intended to say, they ask those standing nearby for clarification. (7.61)
Placing the vessel in their mouths, they carry it away pitilessly;
being intoxicated, they embrace another man while their own husband is drunk and clinging to another woman.
In the very same way, a man also, joined with the intense outburst of passion,
embraces a woman who is not a woman, due to his delusion regarding women.
Deluded, they ask their own husband: "Who are you? Who am I? What is this eye? What is our purpose? Why have we come? For what reason are we standing here? (7.64)
Is this a garden, or a ruined house, or perhaps a courtyard?
The women make their lovers drink wine from their mouths until they are full.
Having placed a snack in her own mouth, she puts it into the mouth of her beloved;
the woman of Śambhu places their vessels and side dishes for one another to take.
Placing wine-vessels upon their heads, the yoginīs dance,
performing a song whose rhythm and tempo are unknown and whose syllables are untouched by conventional phonetics.
The Kula-Śāktas dance with stumbling steps,
and the Yogins, intoxicated by their own pride, fall upon the breasts of women.
And the yoginīs, agitated by passion, fall upon the chest of the man, fulfilling one another's desires. (7.69)
O Mistress of the Kula, they perform various such gestures, having abandoned any agitation of the mind, so that spiritual rapture may proceed. (7.70)
At that time, the best of yogis attain the state of divinity;
whereas the fool-minded person who reviles the Kaulikas, who are possessed by Bhairava, [falls]. (7.71)
Therefore, there is no doubt that the Yoginīs, the leaders of the Kula, will nourish him;
the Kaulas in the circle, though agitated by intoxication, should neither revile nor laugh at them.
One should not disclose to outsiders the news concerning this wheel;
one should not harbor malice toward them, nor should one act in their detriment. (7.73)
One should protect one's livelihood with devotion and guard it with great effort;
seeing a woman intoxicated with passion, one should regard her with the thought that she is a deity.
O Dear One, the Kaulika, rejoicing and bowing with devotion, shall go to the station of the Yoginī;
he beholds the Lord in this manner through devotion to the Cakra.
The fruit of millions of vows, sacred fords, austerities, gifts, and sacrifices shall be attained;
likewise, there is the rising from falling and the repeated occurrence of fainting by one whose mind has transcended [the senses] (unmanāḥ). (7.76)
In that sixth [state] called Unmanā, which is radiant and endowed with heroes, these two syllables *ya* and *ca* grant perpetual presence. 7.77.
O Mistress of the Kula, those who desire the investigation of the Supreme Brahman are said to be perpetually without control over their bodies and senses, and lacking stability. (7.78)
O beloved, when this seventh chapter, which describes other states, is recited,
he becomes one whose nature is the supreme mantra, intent upon the musical mode (mūrchanā).
In the wheel of Bhairavī, all castes become twice-born;
in the wheel of Bhairavī, all castes cease to exist as distinct entities.
Whether it be a woman, a man, a eunuch, an outcaste, or the best of the twice-born—within the center of the Wheel there is no distinction; all are remembered as equal to the gods.
Just as the water of rivers such as the Nirjhara attains oneness upon reaching the Gaṅgā,
so too do human beings attain oneness within the center of the Śrīcakra.
Just as water mixed with milk becomes milk itself, so too within the Śrīcakra, no distinction of caste exists. (7–83)
Just as there are no gods other than those in the meritorious worlds such as Svarga,
so too within the Cakra, all deities are merely human beings.
No distinction of caste exists; all are remembered as equal to Śiva.
Indeed, this is established even in the Veda, for it declares that "all is Brahman. (7–85)
What need is there for much speaking here, O Kuleśvarī? Within the circle, all men are of your form, and all women, O beloved, are of your form.
O Mistress of the Kula, the Yoginīs devour that deluded soul who creates distinctions of caste within the center of the wheel. (7–87)
One should have one woman and one man sit separately in their respective places, or else, having formed a pair, one should have them sit down together in due order.
O Dear One, whether in the form of a row or correctly in the form of a circle,
one should worship everything within the center of the wheel with the consciousness of Śiva and Śakti.
Just as we two, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, are inseparable, O beloved,
so too are Vīrī and Śatānanda, as well as Vīra together with his Śakti.
Neither without having bathed, nor while remaining seated, nor after eating— even at the time of dissolution—
nor unless one is adorned with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, auspicious garments, and so forth.
One should not perform the worship of the lineage without having set aside the body;
for that worship which is without mantra, and that libation which is without mantra, [is ineffective]. (7.92)
O Dear One, it is said that drinking [wine] without the power of destruction (vināśa-śakti) is fruitless;
one should not perform the rite alone in the Śrīcakra, nor should one worship in a single vessel.
One should not worship with only one hand, nor drink with a single hand;
O Goddess, one should not worship with fish, meat, or fermented liquors in the presence of animals.
Having prostrated, one should enter the Śrīcakra, and having prostrated again, one should depart;
one should remain seated upon the Śrīcakra, and likewise not in the vīrāsana posture.
O Goddess, the vision of the Śrīcakra destroys the sins of the eyes;
yet if that [vision] does not exist, then the pair of eyes of a Kaulika is merely a pair of sores.

O Goddess, one should contemplate those who follow improper conduct, those of good conduct, those established in the *cakra*, and the *śakti-kaulikās* as being Śiva and Gaurī; one should not despise them. (7.97)
Having gone to the house of the family preceptor, one should with devotion request for nectar-like food for the purification of sins; in its absence, one should drink water.
Having paid homage, one should receive it; otherwise, one would go to hell.
O Mistress of the Kula, even if one has not bathed, or has already eaten, or is without devotion, [one should still receive it].
He who uses your family property shall always fall into poverty;
he shall be shorn of his turban, wearing a bodice, naked, with disheveled hair, and with a garland hanging from his neck.
One who is averse [to the teachings] and contentious should not serve the nectar of the lineage;
for by spitting out the nectar of yoga, one wanders through the vessels of liquor.
One who weeps, or consumes food and drink [in such a manner], shall incur the curse of the deities;
as shall those who sit upon a single seat or eat from a single vessel.
Those who drink with only one hand go to the realm dear to the denizens of hell;
so too does he who consumes the family property while his teacher resides in the same village.
O Mistress of the Kula, he who acts toward a knower of the Kula, or toward his son, or toward his own eldest teacher, without permission, shall go to an inexhaustible hell. (7.104)
O Pārvatī, one who is impure from remnants of food must not touch the ritual implements or the substances of the Kula;
having washed both hands outside, one should then offer the Kula substances.
O Dear One, having lifted the vessel for liquor, one should not fill it with [other] vessels;
nor should one ever cast the vessel for enjoyment into the jar of wine.
Indeed, that deluded soul who, with a mind impure, performs the washing of hands and other such acts within the center of the *cakra*, shall become a vessel for calamities. (7.107)
He who voids excrement, impurity, or urine within the Śrīcakra, or releases wind within it, shall become a beast among yoginīs. (7.108)

O Beloved, when the jar in the center of the cakra is broken, or when the vessel slips, or when the lamp goes out—for the sake of pacifying these [obstacles]—one should have the Śrīcakra constructed, O Beloved. (7.109)
They mutter, they meditate, they praise, and they prostrate;
they weep and they desire women, O beloved, weeping out of ignorance. (7.110)
One should avoid joking, idle chatter, caviling, excessive talk, indifference, fear, and anger in the midst of the assembly. (7.111)
O Great Goddess, with the vessel in his hand, he should wander within the circle of the mandala;
holding the vessel with both hands, O Beloved, he should remain there for a long time.
O Ambikā, one should not shake the bowl held in the hand, nor should one break the bowl;
one should not touch the bowl with the feet, nor should one let a drop fall to the ground.
One should not give with only one hand, nor should one drink without the *mudrā*.
One should not move the vessel from its place, nor should one cause the vessel to be disturbed.
One should not drink liquor making a sound, nor likewise fill [the vessel] to the brim;
one should not strike one vessel against another, nor let a vessel fall to the ground.
One should not lift the vessel without its base, nor should one cast it down without a support.
One should not leave the vessel empty, nor should one swing it about, O beloved. (7.116)
The wise one should not leap over the vessel, nor should he shake the vessel, O beloved;
having washed it, he should conceal the vessel—this is the command of the Supreme Goddess. (7.117)
When the Kaulika, blazing with radiant splendor, looks upon a bound soul (paśu), or reads the scriptures of the bound souls, or associates with the women of the bound souls; || 7-118 ||

If one indulges in sexual intercourse with animals or performs acts pertaining to animals, the attainment of dharma, wealth, fame, and character, as well as knowledge, happiness, and so forth, will perish. (7.119)
He who gives the ritual substance (kuladravya) of the Śrīcakra to the uninitiated (paśus), whether out of affection, greed, or even fear, shall become a beast (paśu) to the Yoginīs. (7.120)
One should not engage in verbal dispute even with an enemy while in the midst of the assembly;
one should regard them as equal to one's father or mother, and should endure their touch without speaking.
Just as the mind becomes impassioned upon seeing a woman, a son, a friend, or others, so too, if one sees a Kaulika, he shall become dear to the Yoginī. (7.122)
On this earth, who would not revere me, a disciple of one whose lineage of gurus extends from Brahmā down to a blade of grass?
He whose mind is thus resolved shall be dear to us both—he who is arrogant, thinking, "I am the teacher," "I am the elder," and "I am the knower. (7.124)
Those whose minds are such as mine, they are not Kaulikas;
[they do not honor] the venerable Guru, the Kula scriptures, and those places worthy of worship. (7.125)
O Goddess, having bowed down with devotion preceded by "Śrī," one should proclaim [the name];
O Beloved, one should not address the Guru by name except at the time of recitation (japa).
In a dispute or for the purpose of awakening [the disciple], one should say: "Śrīnātha Deva Svāmī.
[One should also recite] the Śrīguru, the Pādukā, the Mudrā, the Mūlamantra, and one's own Pādukā. (7.127)
O Goddess, one should not speak of this to anyone other than a disciple;
O Beloved, the mantras and the traditional transmission of the lineage sequence [are to be kept secret]. (7.128)
Everything obtained from the mouth of the Guru shall be fruitful, and not otherwise.
O Dear One, a book that has come into being through reliance on the venerable scripture is a deity.
One should always worship with devotion and deposit [the offerings] in the house of the bound soul (paśu);
one should study the Kula scriptures like one's own wife, O Pārvatī. (7.130)
One should avoid all animal-science treatises as one would another's wife;
just as milk contained within its own hide cannot be drunk by the best of Brahmins, so too [should these texts be avoided]. (7.131)
Likewise, the dharma of the animal-faced [deities] must not be heard by the Kaulikas;
yet he who hears the Kula conduct and speaks it according to the scripture [is one to be honored]. (7.132)
Both of them go directly to the assembly of Yoginīs and Vīras,
O Kuleśvarī, even if they lack faith in this family dharma.
They do not return from hell until the dissolution of all beings;
though they have grown, been sustained, and found pleasure there, they were not brought back by their price.
Even if they have once entered the realm of desire, the wives of the guru are of five kinds and are not to be transgressed; the wives of the guru are to be honored just like the guru himself.

One should not desire a Guru’s consort, a hero’s consort, a virgin, or one who observes vows; nor should one desire one with deformed limbs, one with mutilated limbs, or even one who is wicked. (7.136)
One should not cause one's own sister, daughter, daughter-in-law, or even the wife of a brother to embrace the preceptor in his presence; rather, one should have another woman perform the embracing.
One should worship with the thought that she is a deity— a maiden who is dark or fair, of dark complexion, slender-waisted, heart-stealing, and in the prime of youth.
One should never, even once, serve a Kulayoginī by force;
O Mistress of the Kula, one should desire her who is herself aroused within the center of the Cakra.
A jar of raw meat and wine, an intoxicated elephant, a linga of supernatural power, a mango tree, an aśoka tree, and young maidens eager for play.
Upon seeing a solitary tree, a cremation ground, a gathering of women,
or a woman dressed in red garments, one should pay homage with devotion.
The Guru, Śakti, the son, the eldest, those established in the Kula, the teachers,
the scriptures of the Kula-darśana, the Kula-substances, and the Kaulikas.

The Yoginī [bestows] those who incite, those who indicate, as well as those who speak, those who illuminate, those who instruct, those who awaken, and those who possess human perfection and spiritual success.
One should not rejoice over, nor feel aversion toward, nor laugh at, nor insult girls, young maidens, naked women, or even those who are insane. (7.144)
One should not speak unpleasantly or falsely to any member of a family of yogis; nor should one say of a woman of such a family, "She is ill-favored" or "She is black-footed. (7.145)
One should examine the eating of the sky by heroes, whether it has been done or not;
one should not look at a woman who has fallen, who is submerged, who is insane, or whose breasts are exposed. (7.146)
Just as one would look at a river, so should one look upon the womb of whatever woman there may be in the world who has been born from her mother’s lineage. (7.147)
The family yoginīs become enraged by the transgression against women;
one should not strike even a hundred women, whether they be others' wives or strangers, even with a flower.
One should count the faults of women but never reveal their virtues;
the Kula-yoginīs always abide within the Kula-trees. (7.149)
One should not eat from leaves, especially not from arka leaves; one should not sleep beneath a kula-tree, nor should one expose oneself to calamities and the like.
Having seen [it], one should bow with devotion; one should never cut it down.
[The following trees are prohibited: the *śleṣmātaka*, the *karañja*, the *akṣa*, the *nimba*, the *aśvattha*, and the *kadaṃbaka*.
The bilva, the vaṭa, the udumbara, and the ciñcā—these ten are recorded [as forbidden fruits].
[The following are also prohibited: the expiation of Bhṛgu, suicide by falling from a precipice, renunciation, and the observance of vows.
A Kaula should avoid these five: going on pilgrimages, killing a Vīra, drinking in vain, and the theft of a Vīra’s substance.
Sexual intercourse with the wife of a hero, and being joined with her as the fifth—
this is declared to be a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) in the Kula scriptures of the Kaulikas.
In the Śaiva [tradition], the thorough knowledge of the principles (tattvas) is the essence; in the Gāruḍa, the swallowing of poison;
in Jyotiṣa, the planetary eclipses; and in Kaula, the favoring and subjugating of others.
One who mocks the deities, the guru, the scriptures, and the conduct of the perfected ones (siddhas), a thief of knowledge, and a traitor to the guru, shall become a brahmarākṣasa. (7.156)
O Goddess, one should slay without hesitation that person who reviles one's mother, father, wife, brothers, kinsmen, or preceptor. (7.157)
Internally Kaula, externally Śaiva, and throughout one's life Vaiṣṇava— one should keep the Kaula secret,
O Goddess, like the water inside a coconut fruit.
O Goddess, this is the family dharma; in all circumstances and at all times, one should guard it with effort, like the secret of one's mother’s paramour and her pregnancy.
The Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas have been touched like courtesans;
but this knowledge of Shambhu is hidden like a woman of noble family.
The deities bestow their grace upon those whose Kaula conduct is well-guarded; they grant the attainment of one's desires and destroy those who reveal [the secrets]. (7.161)
O beloved, in the scriptures expiations are seen for those who have committed great sins;
however, O Goddess of gods, no expiation is seen anywhere for one who has fallen from his lineage.
O beloved, for that great sinner who, relying on his family dharma, does not maintain proper conduct and wanders according to his own whims— 7.163.
Calamities arise, diseases, poverty, strife, and fear;
there is the wrath of the Yoginīs and stumbling at every step. (7.164)
Therefore, O Goddess, one who possesses proper conduct shall be dear to the Yoginīs.
In the Rudrayāmala, all the scriptures, the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, and ascetic penances [are contained therein]. (7-165)
O beautiful one, sacrifices, fire-offerings, pilgrimages, and various kinds of gifts become fruitless here for those who follow the path of the beasts.
There is no dharma equal to Kaula; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt, O Mistress of Kula, regarding the high-souled Kaulikas who are established in Kula. (7.167)
I shall grant supreme knowledge by my own will; of this there is no doubt.
O twice-born ones, all have been declared as Śākta; they are neither Śaivas nor Vaiṣṇavas.
"They worship the Primordial Goddess Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Vedas.
Thus concludes the description of the family tradition (kulācāra). Now follows the description of the wheels (cakras).
In the Rudrayāmala, the venerable Goddess said:
"O God of gods, O Lord of the world, you who are proficient in all branches of knowledge! (7.169)
"O Lord, for the benefit of the Kaulikas, speak of the divisions of the Cakras.
The Lord said: "In the Śrītantra Rudrayāmala, the Cakra is declared to be fivefold."
One should worship the wheel according to the prescribed rule for the attainment of the fruits of happiness and liberation:
the Royal Wheel, the Great Wheel, and furthermore, the Divine Wheel. (7.171)
The Vīracakra shall be the fourth, while the Paśucakra is the fifth.
O Pārvatī, listen as I describe the materials for worship in the Rājacakra.
Horses of the four castes that are handsome and very charming;
or, in their absence, one should worship any young maidens according to the prescribed rite.
The Yavanī, the Yoginī, the Rajakī, the Pacī, and she born of a Kaivarta—these are declared to be the five Śaktis. (7.174)
All these, when employed by the practitioner and consecrated with mantra, are praised as bestowers of the fruits of all desires. (7.175)
Honey-wine is fully prescribed, and purification is derived from goats;
fish is said to be that of the uddālaka species, and the mudrā is known to be made from wheat.
One should employ flowers and sandalwood in the royal circle,
especially on the eleventh lunar day, on Sundays, and at the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign.
The wheel of kings is ordained for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
having fashioned the wheel, one should indeed bestow it as a sacrificial fee upon the guru.
O lord of the earth, for sixty thousand years, those practitioners shall dwell in the world of the gods, receiving auspicious [rewards] according to their capacity and as appropriate for the time.
Thus concludes the description of the royal circle.
Īśvara said: O Pārvatī, listen with devotion as I shall proclaim the Mahācakra.
[The women] are the mother, the sister, the daughter, and likewise the wife. (7.180)
The teacher’s wife—these five are recorded as the Śaktis in the *Yāmala*.
Śrī Pārvatī said: "O Goddess, having approached the mother, one should sport with her by means of the eye. (7.181)
"In that regard, O Śaṅkara, where does the construction for the deity reside?
Īśvara said:
"The wife of the initiated guru, who bore the child in her womb, is the mother. (7.182)
If one marries a maiden who does not satisfy [the ancestors] nor provide enjoyment for them—be she a sister, a daughter, the wife of a hero, or likewise a daughter-in-law—[he incurs sin]. (7.183)
Others should be avoided with effort, yet they may be used for enjoyment;
the syllable is said to be that of the Gaudas, while purity arises from the Kukkutas.
The rohita fish is prescribed, as well as those produced from mūdrā and māṣa beans;
likewise, the flower produced from karavīra, sandalwood, and red sandalwood.
O Goddess, one should present the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to the prescribed rite;
[thereby] one rejoices together with Brahmā for sixty thousand years.
On Thursday and Friday, on the fourth and seventh lunar days,
O Maheśānī, the Mahācakra bestows the prosperity of all cakras.
Thus ends the section on the great wheels.
I shall now describe the divine wheel of Īśvara, which is always performed by the gods.
Being capable in that regard, I shall describe the goddesses who possess beautiful forms.
O beloved, the royal courtesan (rājaveśyā), the various women (nānārī), the secret courtesan (guptaveśyā),
the divine courtesan (devaveśyā), and the brahmin courtesan (brahmaveśyā) are proclaimed as the five Śaktis.
The royal courtesan is devoted to the service of kings and remains concealed;
the divine courtesan is a dancer; and the spiritual courtesan frequents sacred pilgrimage sites. (7.190)
Nāgarī is someone’s maiden; Raṇḍā is agitated by the essence of desire.
O Goddess, one should employ these five Śaktis in the wheel of the gods. (7.191)
The syllable is said to be produced from grain, while the mudrās are derived from chickpeas;
one should know the flower to be the *cāṃ* [seed], and whatever excellent fragrance there may be as the drink. (7.192)
Having placed it before the teacher, one should present it as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
for sixty thousand years, one rejoices in the realm of the King of the Gods.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth lunar days; on Tuesdays and Mondays; and when the remaining [auspicious] conjunctions have arrived, it is declared to be most excellent.
Thus ends the section on the wheels of the gods.
The Lord said: I shall now proclaim the Vīracakra, by means of which practitioners attain accomplishment.
O Goddess, through this worship, the perfection of the body is produced. (7.195)

The practitioner who is well-established should offer fish, wine, and other such things that are praised as the powers (śaktis) of those who move on earth and those who move in the sky, provided they are not meat. (7.196)
O Supreme Goddess, all the previously mentioned mudrās are praised;
likewise, white, yellow, and especially red flowers [are recommended]. (7.197)
O twice-born one, one should arrange the eight heroes, the six heroes, and likewise the nine heroes; and one should also arrange the rows of heroes as they are obtained, O beautiful one.
One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the heroes and present them to the teacher;
indeed, even the countless sins, such as the sin of killing a Brahmin, [are purified]. (7.199)
O Goddess, by the power of the Vīracakra, it destroys [all obstacles] in that very instant;
however, if the ritual of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is omitted, that cakra becomes fruitless.
Thus concludes the exposition on the Vīracakra.

The Lord said: O Daughter of the Mountain, I shall now describe the wheel of bound souls (paśucakra), which is indeed characterized by unrighteousness; in this [wheel], one indulges in drinking, eating, and sexual pleasure. (7.201)
O beloved, he who drinks liquor alone and eats meat alone never forms an association with a devotee of Maheśvara.
For the sake of one's own pleasure, [one consumes] liquor, meat, and likewise fish;
yet there is the exhaustion of life and poverty, and upon death, one shall go to the state of a *piśāca*. (7.203)
One may remain in the circle of Piśācas for sixty thousand years;
thus ends the section on the circle of Paśus.
Īśvara said: The Rājacakra consists of the Rājadaṃśas; it is the Mahācakra that brings about illumination.
The Vīracakra bestows accomplishment (siddhi), while the Devacakra grants prosperity;
however, the Paśucakra brings about poverty and the loss of longevity.
If the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is deficient due to deceit, the entire ritual cycle becomes futile. || 7-205ef ||
Thus ends the description of the five wheels in the *Kaularahasya*,
concerning those who are intent upon the libation of Śrī Sundarī and whose eyes are rolling with wine.
May the days pass for us, the devotees of Maheśvara, with our minds filled with joy.
Day after day may there be jars full of *sīdhu*; day after day may there be libations for the Goddess;
day after day may a second [consort] arise; day after day may there be union with the fifth.
These categories of reality are capable of rescuing those sinking in the midst of the ocean of existence:
the five-syllabled mantra of the Supreme Deity, the goddess Śīlavatī, and the messenger Dūtī. (7.208)
Nor is there the tasting of cool water; here, even that leaf with five syllables cannot be found.
Where there is no attachment for those with deer-like eyes, such a day is a dark day—so say others.

O Mother, for those intent upon your worship, the splendor of the celestial wish-fulfilling tree resides in their lotus-like hands; the garlands of the crowns of kings rest upon their lotus-like feet; and the sweet speech of the gods flows from their lotus-like mouths. (7.210)

If the lotus-feet are in the hand, if they are in the heart, or if they are on the head, then that which is in the lotus-face is the nectar to be drunk; who are the wise ones [else], and who are we? (7.211)

Having consumed *hālā* in the temples of the initiated and slept at night in the houses of courtesans, he should perform the chewing [of the sacramental substance] in every house; thus the sovereign of the Kaulas shines resplendent. (7.212)
Indeed, there is no enjoyment of the vessel where there is liberation, and where there is liberation, there is indeed no enjoyment.
But for those intent on the propitiation of Śrī Sundarī, both enjoyment and liberation are held in the very palm of their hand.
Embracing the young woman with his left arm and drinking wine together with her, holding a vessel in his lotus-like right hand, he should fix his mind upon the Supreme Deity. (7.214)
In this ocean of worldly existence, which is devoid of essence, a truly great effort has been made by me;
now, through the grace of the feet of my Lord, the Kaula path—the very gateway to liberation—has been embraced. (7.215)
Having fashioned a stream of nectar from her mouth and fragments of purity within that interval,
Śrīsundarī bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those people who meditate on these two aspects of her face.
Blessed indeed is that Ādinātha who for a long time has resorted to the path of liberation of the Kaulas;
in whom virtues become faults, sins become merits, and worldly enjoyments become like dirt on the hands.
Śyāmā alone is Rāmā; the learned man alone is a kinsman; knowledge alone is a friend; the bow alone is a weapon;
the Gaṅgā alone is a sacred ford; Smara alone is an archer; and among paths, the path of Maheśvara alone is the true path.
And if this supreme deity protects me with her compassionate glances, then talk of the great trees of the kalpas and the thought of the wish-fulfilling gem is in vain. (7.219)
In the *Śrī Kulārṇava*, I am one devoted to the enjoyment and worship of the city of hundreds of women; I am honored as the initiator of the manifold paths of the Kula.
I am averse to the world of the fettered (paśu); I have taken refuge in Bhairavī; I am devoted to the feet of the Guru. I am Bhairava; I am Śiva. (7.220)
In her left hand is a woman skilled in amorous play, and in her right a vessel of wine; she holds roasted chickpea cakes and excellent meat.
There is the lute, the sweet sound of poetry, the noble stories of true gurus, and the Kaula dharma—most profound and inaccessible even to yogis. (7.221)

Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Kulapradīpa* composed by the venerable Śivānandācārya. May there be auspiciousness! On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha in the year 1788, on Tuesday—may it be auspicious! The number of verses is 1,800.
